en: The Vinaya Sūtra (VinSū 3) [1. The Chapter on Going Forth]
[(i) The Ordination into the State of a Śrāmaṇera] // Homage to the Omniscient One!
For the sake of compendium, that Guṇaprabha composed these sūtras of the Vinaya; this commentary on them is now being declared.
In this regard, the first sūtra is as follows: (1) Now, the section on the departure [from saṃsāra].
The word "atha" (now) serves to indicate the commencement of a new topic.
It should be understood that from this point until the conclusion of the composition of the sūtra, the subject matter under discussion is the conduct of departure (*niryāṇavṛtta*).
Here, "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to attainment, not movement.
"Niryāṇa" means that by means of this, one goes forth;
it is like saying "one who has reached the village.
The prefix *niḥ* is used for the purpose of indicating non-return.
The phrase "the vehicle that does not lead to returning" refers to the remainder, namely, the departure [from saṃsāra].
This is stated because of the attainment of nirvāṇa without remainder.
Is that indeed the vehicle that does not lead to returning?
Now, as for the question "What is it?"— it is called "departure" (*niryāṇa*) because they depart from that.
By this term, it is not understood that the attainment of *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) is what is being described here.
If it is argued that "it is called the path (mārga) because one goes forth by means of it," [we reply:
since the word *niḥ* has not come here with the sense of "commencement" (*upakramaṇa*), nor with the sense of "termination" (*paryanta*).
Based on this, there is the teaching of nirvana with remainder.
Therefore, this vehicle is the departure, the going forth,
or the reaching of the limit of the course of cyclic existence;
and he has not relied upon that [course].

What, then, is intended here by the word "soundless" (*niḥśabda*)? It is intended in the sense of "non-return. Therefore, by this [term], only that vehicle which brings about non-return is spoken of, and no other.

And because, having reached a certain level of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), one attains *nirvāṇa* with a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
When one emerges from that stage and proceeds to another stage, that is not a "return";
rather, falling away from the state of an Arhat and so forth is indeed a disappearance.
Furthermore, in this context, "vehicle" (yāna) refers to the attainment of the path,
not the act of traveling.
Therefore, because it does not rely on the meaning of "going," there is no consequence of its being a departure.
The conduct that leads to departure is the conduct of departure.
Furthermore, regarding the *vṛtta* (conduct) here for those who uphold the Dharma:
whatever conduct there is, it should be understood as having been taught in its entirety by the Vinaya.

Therefore, herein [the topics are]: ordination (*pravrajyā*), the analysis of offenses (*vibhaṅga*), the *poṣadha*, the rainy season retreat (*varṣa*), the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), the wooden robe frame (*kaṭhina*), robes (*cīvara*), skins (*carma*), medicines (*bhaiṣajya*), formal acts (*karman*), counter-measures (*pratikriyā*), appropriate and inappropriate times (*kāla-akāla-sampāta*), the conduct of one staying in another territory (*bhūmyantara-sthacaraṇa*), purification (*parikarma*), schism in the formal act (*karmabheda*), schism in the assembly (*cakrabheda*), legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), and the matter of lodgings (*śayanāsana-vastu*)—in this sequence.
The arrangement of the entire system of discipline (*vinaya-vidhi*).
For this is the intended meaning here: "By this method, the acquisition of going-forth (*pravrajyā*) and full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) is proper;
and there is an inclusion here of those very persons of such a kind."
Such individuals as these are to be avoided here;
since it is appropriate to speak of this first, the section on "Going Forth" (*pravrajyā*) is placed at the beginning.
For one who has entered the teaching but has not yet attained the conduct (*vṛtta*) herein, there is this training (*śikṣā*), consisting of the expulsion from training and so forth.
Therefore, immediately following this, comes the arrangement of the Vibhaṅga.

These are the reasons for the sequence of the *poṣadhavastu* and the others: nourishment (*paripoṣaṇa*), such as [the periodic] refreshing of the training one has undertaken by relying on the Sūtra from time to time;
therefore, the *poṣadhavastu* is mentioned first.

Because the accomplishment of one's purpose occurs through staying together at one place, the rule regarding that state of staying is the *varṣavastu* (the matter of the rainy season retreat). Following that,

since the giving of the formal relinquishment (*utsarga*) is appropriate when purity has been established by means of the three grounds— namely, what has been seen, heard, and suspected— at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat which consists of a fixed residence, the *pravāraṇāvastu* (the matter of the invitation ceremony) follows immediately after.
He possesses a certain arrangement of the meditative posture (*vyūhabandha*) which serves as a protective cloak for his settled dwelling during the rainy season retreat;

it is to be relied upon for the sake of abiding in pliancy (*prasrabdhi*). Immediately following this, the sequence of that [practice] is established as the section on the "Hard Object" (*kaṭhinavastu*).

Since there is no application for the distribution of robes in that case where there is no offense, and because the time for giving robes is when those two types of military arrays have been withdrawn, this is the basis for the rule concerning robes.
Following the section on hides—which is a specific classification of robes—the section on hides (*carmavastu*) has been inserted.

Since it is not possible for one person, whether alone or with another, to dwell without the remedy for illness, there is generally a state of falling ill at the very first time of giving robes, due to the proximity of the preceding and succeeding periods of time.
Because it is directed toward that [sickness] and is endowed with the proper form of remedial treatment, it is called the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Section on Medicines).
This is the procedure for the performance of duties as they arise for those dwelling in this manner;
immediately following this is the section on ritual actions (karmavastu).

The restraint of those who have become unruly—such as those deserving of disciplinary action—and their restoration through the performance of penance and so forth, as well as their removal through banishment and other means, are appropriate; therefore, this is the "matter of remedial action."

The arrangement for the purpose of regulating and restoring one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense— concerning the matter of conduct while staying in another territory during times both appropriate and inappropriate—
is stated under the names of the *kauśāmbaka*, *pāṇḍulohitaka*, and *pudgalaparivāsika* matters, as well as the matter of remedial action (*pratikriyāvastu*) and so forth.
We shall explain the purpose of assigning these alternative designations in that very sequence.
Since it is appropriate to first subdue those who approach for the sake of discipline and so forth, this is the section on preliminary services (*parikarmavastu*).

This is another designation for the matter of the suspension of the *poṣadha*; it refers to what occurs among those who have split into two factions, and this constitutes the matter of the schism in the wheel of the Dharma (*karmacakra-bheda*).
Therefore, the procedure pertaining to legal proceedings is appropriate immediately after this;
such is the subject matter of this section.
Since this entire range of wholesome practices is performed in that place, it is appropriate that this rule applies to one who has gone there; thus, the matter of bedding and seating is established.
Since these [factors] such as the minor ones (kṣudraka) are merely subdivisions of those [already mentioned], they do not exceed them; therefore, they are not set forth in a separate sūtra.
Wherever one’s application lies, there alone it is established.

Immediately after receiving permission from the *ācārya* and *upādhyāya*, regarding the procedure for the initiation (*pravrajyā*) and the leading forward (*upanaya*), he says—(2)—in order to demonstrate that:
when the entire Saṃgha has assembled, having assumed the proper attire, prostrated, and with palms joined, one stands in a squatting position at the end of the senior monks.
They should lead one who has made the request through the formal act consisting of three announcements and a fourth motion to both the going forth and full ordination; such was the ancient rule.
The word "in all" is used for the purpose of prohibiting the gathering of even a portion of the Saṃgha within a single maṇḍalaka.
Nor [is it valid] even when [the Saṃgha] is located within a single part of a maṇḍala; rather, it must be all [the members] residing within its internal boundary (sīmā).
"By him this dress was made"— thus, "those by whom this dress was made" (kṛtedaveṣāḥ).
"This" refers to the designation of one who wears the robes of a monk according to the Buddha's teaching;
the meaning is that he has removed his hair and beard and is clad in the saffron-colored monastic robe (*cīvara*).
"Having prostrated" refers to what will be stated later as "in the presence of the elders."
And its connection is as follows:
the meaning is that, having prostrated at the end of the elders' row, one performs a salutation by means of the five-pointed prostration (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*).
"With hands joined" means having made the gesture of añjali.
"Standing in the utkuṭuka posture" means remaining in the utkuṭuka position;
it does not mean seated upon a seat.
To the question "Where is he standing?", he says: "at the end of the assembly of elders."

Now, one might ask: since the rule that "one who is seated in the *utkuṭuka* posture at the edge of the assembly with palms joined" was formulated in the *Paribhāṣā* section as applicable to all formal acts (*karma*) dependent upon the Saṅgha, why is it stated again here—given that this triad [of postures] is already obtained because it is a formal act—as well? [The answer is: because of the statement, "the palms are joined due to being concerned with the present eon," and so forth; from this *paribhāṣā*, there is the declaration that its establishment here pertains to the ancient eon (*purākalpa*).
What is it that one has requested?
It is the going forth (pravrajyā) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Furthermore, the request is as follows: “May [the Venerable One] listen...”
"Venerable Saṃgha, I, named so-and-so, desire the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣu within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya," and so on in detail.

"By this mantra, having requested three times, by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth [proclamation]"—that formal act in which there are three proclamations following a motion is a "formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth"; by that.
"Simultaneous with the going forth and the full ordination" means that the going forth and the full ordination occur at the same time,
not sequentially.
"They should bring them" means the monks who have formed a Saṃgha.
And thus the mantra: “May the venerable Saṃgha listen:

this one named so-and-so desires the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may the Saṃgha grant the going forth and the full ordination to this one named so-and-so.”
Such was the ancient tradition.
The word *iti* expresses a manner or mode.
"In a former age" (purākalpe) means prior to the present kalpa; the meaning is that the procedure for going forth and receiving full ordination was of such a kind [in the past].
If it is asked: "Why was this very present kalpa not previously designated by the Blessed One;
why was this rule not established earlier, but rather formulated again now, setting aside former kalpas?"—it is because those practitioners at that time were beings of pure nature.
For them, there is no need for gradual discipline, nor training through the support of others;
they experience no weariness.
Because they have performed meritorious deeds, what is non-existent does not come to pass for them; or, even if such things were to occur, they themselves become compassionate.
This is because, at that time, there was no transgression regarding obstructive factors (*āntarāyika-dharma*).
Thus, the designation of "former kalpas" (*purākalpa*) is made with respect to those who have departed from this world.
But when these have arisen in another manner, then there is no utility whatsoever for the subsequent presentation;
what is the point of including this here?
Even if, according to this method, there is currently no practical application, [it remains relevant].
Nevertheless, there is no difference between this and the answer; that which is a distinction later on is merely its supplementary equipment.
In this regard, here is the mantra-tantra:
It was merely this much; it was only a pair.
This composition was made for the purpose of explaining the meaning that the establishment of another rule of this kind occurs by virtue of the Vinaya.
Thus has the ancient tradition been shown together with its purpose.
Now, regarding the present eon, it is said:
(3) [He ordained] a certain monk who was dependent upon him as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) for both going forth (*pravrajyā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Regarding the phrase "a certain bhikṣu":

the word "a certain" is used not necessarily to indicate that one must receive full ordination (upasaṃpad) from the very same person from whom one went forth (pravrajyā); rather, it is said to show that [ordination] may be from someone else.
To the question "In what manner does one rely [on him]? he says: "By way of being the preceptor (upādhyāya)."
To the question "For what purpose is it for one who has relied [on others]?", he says: "In that regard.
This refers to the expectation of going forth and full ordination; furthermore, this is a locative case used in the sense of a causal condition (*nimitta-saptamī*).
The going forth and full ordination occur for one who has relied upon a certain monk as preceptor (upādhyāya) for the sake of receiving the going forth and full ordination;
it is not as in former kalpas, when they occurred for someone without relying on anyone at all.
Furthermore, "going forth" (pravrajyā) here should be understood as being followed by the conduct of an Arhat and the novice's restraint (śrāmaṇerasaṃvara);
for both going forth and the novice's restraint depend upon this [ordination].
Furthermore, the distinction here is that the going forth is from the preceptor alone, whereas the restraint is from another.
He states the rule for the dependence of one who is dependent upon being accepted by a preceptor: (4)

Having asked about the obstructing factors, he should grant the initial opportunity to one who is pure; for "obstructing factors" here refers to those things that create an obstacle to going forth, such as the killing of one's mother and so forth. Therefore, this preceptor, having asked about the obstructing factors concerning the candidate for going forth, [should act].

If those qualities do not exist in him, then for that person who is completely pure, one should grant permission to act as his former preceptor (*pūrvopādhyāya*) or as a novice preceptor (*śrāmaṇeropādhyāya*), saying: "Venerable sir, I shall cause you to go forth.
And thus says the text: "To whomever desiring the going forth approaches..."
"Having been asked by him about the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*), he should accept [the vows].

Showing the sequence of the restraints (*saṃvara*), he said: (5) "For one who has not previously entered [the lower stages], there is no higher [attainment] of the states of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), or a full monk (*bhikṣu*)."

Among these stages, such as that of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth, one should not undertake each subsequent stage without having first attained identity with the preceding stage—which has not been properly accomplished.
This is an explanation of the established order.

Having asked about the obstructing factors, one should first cause the candidate for ordination to undertake the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); thereafter, the status of a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*),
and then the status of a full monk (*bhikṣu*)— this is for the purpose of making him understand this sequence.
But it is not for this reason that the conventional usage of the latter term occurs because it was not previously employed in the former case.
Regarding the establishment of the *bhikṣu* vow even prior to other vows, there is indeed a primary scriptural statement (*mūlavacana*).
However, it is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) that the *śrāmaṇera* vow arises from the *upāsaka* vow;
there is no statement that the *bhikṣu* vow is its refuge (*pratiśaraṇa*).

Showing that the undertaking of the vows is preceded by going for refuge, he says: (6) One should perform the speech of undertaking the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), beginning with the words of accepting the going for refuge.
"Gati" means going.
The acceptance of going for refuge is the "acceptance of going for refuge," as in "I go for refuge to the Buddha," and so forth.
The speech that expresses this is the "speech of the acceptance of going for refuge."
That is his speech.
"Commencement" means the beginning;
he should utter the words of formal acceptance of the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
Who is this? It is the one who undertakes [the vow];
this is the meaning.
Thus the recipient should say: "Pay heed, Venerable One! I, named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, up to [the Sangha], the foremost of assemblies."
"Venerable sir, may you remember me as a lay follower for as long as life lasts;
Venerable sir, please take note of me, who am named so-and-so, [as one who has taken refuge] in the Buddha, and so forth, up to 'the foremost of assemblies.
Teacher, may you remember me as a novice."
These two passages, exactly as they are, should be recited three times.

However, by whoever first recites the going for refuge three times, and thereafter says, "Venerable sir, please accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka)," or "Master, please accept me as a novice (śrāmaṇera)," that person should be understood [as having entered the community].
Because, given that this is the case regarding these two utterances for undertaking the vows, the statement of going for refuge does not at all function as a constituent part [of the vow].

Furthermore, for one who has already previously accepted even the mere act of going for refuge, it would follow that at the time of receiving the vows, the mention of going for refuge would be redundant.
Moreover, this must necessarily be stated at this time in order to manifest the intention toward Nirvana;
for in this way alone does it become a constituent part of both the words for undertaking the vows and the words for going for refuge, and not otherwise.
And without the firmness of the resolve for nirvāṇa, there is no arising of the restraint.
Since restraint is conducive to nirvāṇa,
how then can full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) be established without the statement of going for refuge?
This is not a fault.
Because that meaning is established by the very word *upasaṃpad* itself;
for *upasaṃpad* is characterized by the cessation of all that is not to be done, as it is the approach toward Nirvana in its entirety.
For one who is established in full ordination becomes situated in accordance with nirvāṇa.
The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word "kurvīta" (he should do) is for the purpose of indicating that this must be performed as a matter of personal practice;
what another person here expresses as "instruction" (*śikṣaṇa*) should be understood in that sense, and not as the act of giving and receiving.
It should be understood that even on the *upoṣadha* day, this is a duty to be performed by the practitioner alone.
Some explain that regarding the rule of giving and receiving, it occurs "there" simply through the act of instruction;
however, it should be known that this is their error.
Because the undertaking [of the precepts] is equal.
(7) Immediately following this is the proclamation of the training rules (VinSū 7), [in the form of a formal undertaking].

The phrase "of this" refers to the proclamation of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for the lay follower (*upāsaka*) and the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), respectively, immediately following the formal declaration of their acceptance of the status of a lay follower and a novice monk;
specifically, five rules in the former case and ten rules in the latter.
In what manner? He says: by way of formal undertaking (*abhyupagama-rūpeṇa*).
That is, "I desist from this and that," but not, "This and that which has been undertaken by you must be guarded."
(8) Having personally initiated him into the state of a lay follower, he should entrust him to the Saṃgha for the purpose of reporting [the matter] to the monks.
The word "himself" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), as he is the subject under discussion;
for it is he who has provided the opportunity for that person's going forth.
Having himself brought about the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by bestowing the lay follower's vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*).
To whichever monk reports that person who desires to go forth to the Saṅgha, he should entrust him, saying: "Inform him [of his duties].
This is because, through his connection with the monks, the sense of duty has arisen within him.
The middle voice (ātmanepada) is used for the purpose of demonstrating that this [result] belongs solely to the teacher's own interest.

Because this [act] consists of formal procedures (*karma*) such as a motion (*jñapti*), the announcement to the Saṃgha by one who has not yet received full ordination (*anupasaṃpanna*) regarding someone seeking going-forth (*pravrajyā*) would not be contradictory; therefore, the word "to a monk" (*bhikṣave*) is used in order to exclude that alternative view.
And thus the text says: "Thereafter, a monk should be requested—whosoever shall announce this for him."

The announcer (ārocaka), having asked the preceptor who has presented the candidate, "Is he pure?", should announce one who is pure and seeks ordination by means of the following mantra: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha attend; this person named so-and-so, seeking ordination, has put on white garments," and so forth. As for the use of the middle voice (*parasmaipada*), that is because [the action] is performed through the agency of another.
Because activity is not for its own sake;
for in this case, unlike [the activity] toward a teacher, whose activity is indeed for his own sake as if toward a son, this [activity] is not so.
How should one announce it when the Saṅgha is assembled? He says: (10) either when everyone has gathered or when they are seated in the monastery grounds.
"By way of successive enumeration" is explained as "successive lying down," for a *parigaṇa* is indeed a specific type of shelter.
To demonstrate the procedure for those in whose presence the announcement is made, he says:
(11) "If he is pure," they should all say.
If "sa" has the sense of "yadi" (if),
it means that after the announcement, he becomes one who seeks the going forth.
(12) He should request the preceptor using the formula for requesting; [the preceptor] should have his hair and beard shaved, except for the top-knot.

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the sense that one should cause [the disciple] to enter [the barber’s work] while presiding over him as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), for the purpose of demonstrating the duties of a barber;
however, it should not be thought that this must be performed by the preceptor himself.
Nor should it be considered that what was done through a succession of others is not "done" (*akārita*).
Since activity is for the sake of a purpose,
when that purpose has been accomplished, there is a cessation of activity.

In this regard, once the shaving of the hair and beard has been performed by another without waiting for the teacher's involvement, it should be understood that the teacher must not engage in it again.
"Up to the crest" (*ācūḍam*) means other than the crest (*cūḍā*).
Even when the beard is removed, there is no such perception of deformity as there would be [if the head were shaved].
Therefore, this [shaving] is established for the purpose of discerning whether this [deformity] is certain or not—(14).
When he was asked, "Let the top-knot be removed," and he gave his consent, [the barber] took hold of him.
When the candidate for ordination has been asked, "Let the top-knot be shorn," and if permission is granted by him, then—
once that shaving of the top-knot has been authorized— the instruction "he should have that top-knot shorn" follows. Having thus had his hair and beard shorn, he should bathe.
With water appropriate to the season,
and after the time of bathing,
the preceptor should give him saffron-colored robes.
He too, having prostrated at the feet of the preceptor, accepted it.
Then his own preceptor (upādhyāya) should personally cover him [with the robe]. (VinSū 8)
And while putting it on, in order to avoid the faults of being a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, lacking sexual organs, or possessing both sets of organs,
he should examine his sexual characteristics without premeditation.
And it is not by making him naked,
but rather unintentionally— so that he does not know, "I have been seen by this person"—
for this act is performed through the consent of the preceptor.
Even if it has been performed by another trustworthy monk,
it should be understood as "performed" by the preceptor himself.
(20) One should lead [the candidate] to the going forth, beginning with the taking of refuge.

"By means of this mantra—'I, [named so-and-so], take refuge in the Buddha, up to the foremost of the assemblies; I take upon myself the Blessed One Śākyamuni, up to the marks of renunciation'—the preceptor (upādhyāya) should initiate the going for refuge and lead [the candidate] into the state of renunciation;
the meaning is that this cannot be done without the going for refuge, which serves as the foundation."
Is it not a continuous restraint (*anvaya-saṃvara*)?
Some say that its meaning here consists in being the preliminary stage for going for refuge;
that is incorrect.
Because what is called "going forth" (pravrajyā) is the relinquishing of a dwelling, and all contaminated (sāsrava) things constitute a dwelling for one who takes delight in them.
Therefore, turning away from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the complete abandonment of the household life;
yet, this turning away from cyclic existence is not accomplished by relying on *nirvāṇa* alone.
Consequently, just as in the case of the vows (*saṃvara*), one must here also cultivate the aspiration for *nirvāṇa*; thus, the undertaking of going for refuge is presented even in this context.

Some recite in the mantra for the conferral of the going-forth (*pravrajyā*), prior to the words "I take up the marks of the going-forth" (*pravrajyāliṅgaṃ samādade*), the phrase "May the preceptor recognize me as a novice monk" (*śrāmaṇeraṃ māṃ upādhyāyo dhārayatu*). This is incorrect,
because that which has already grown forth cannot grow again, and because what has already been undertaken cannot be undertaken once more.
It is illogical for the preceptor to recite this mantra [for one who has already received ordination].

Furthermore, in the mantra for the admission into the state of a *śrāmaṇera*, the entry into the wandering life (*pravrajyā*) is also recited by them as follows: "To that Blessed One Śākyamuni... I take up the marks of the wandering life.
For the sake of the goal, I utter the name of my preceptor."
"Thus, may the preceptor accept me as a novice under the name of such-and-such preceptor"—
this is improper, because it is impossible for one who has already undertaken the vows to undertake them again.
(21) "Or immediately after the request. This refers to the phrase "one should lead [the person] to the going forth. The word "or" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of indicating an alternative view.
The reading of some is: "Immediately after the request from the preceptor, one whose hair and beard have not yet been shorn is to be ordained.
Their intention is this: just as the status of a *śrāmaṇera* [is conferred immediately], so too the shaving of hair and other such acts are the duty of one who has already been ordained.
For that very reason, there is a restriction regarding the variation of the text:
in this way, the preceptor of the going-forth should entrust him to a monk who will lead him to the state of a novice.

He who leads one into the state of a śrāmaṇera is called a "śrāmaṇeratvopanāyī" (one who leads into the state of a śrāmaṇera), because it is his nature (*śīla*) to lead one into the state of a śrāmaṇera. That proficiency of mind regarding the formal act of leading one into the restraint (*saṃvara*) of a śrāmaṇera by that leader of the śrāmaṇera-vow— this is [the factor].
It should be understood that [the candidate] has relied [on the teacher] by virtue of his habituation to giving.
To whomsoever it is offered for the purpose of initiation,
he— having asked, "Is this person completely pure?"— should initiate one who is pure.
(24) He is the teacher.
He who leads one to the state of a śrāmaṇera is to be regarded as the preceptor (ācārya).

The *raho'nuśāsaka* (instructor in private), the *karmakāraka* (performer of formal acts), the *niśrayadāyaka* (provider of dependence), and the *pāṭhaka* (reciter) are also [to be understood as] *ācāryas*.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of inclusion.
To what extent do these [mantras] possess the quality of being "arisen" (*jātatva*) as teachers? He says:
(26) "When the object has occurred, there is the state of having come into being.
Thus he says: by means of which object the arrangement of the mantra [is established].
For example, by way of the purpose of being initiated as a novice (śrāmaṇera), when the office of a novice preceptor (śrāmaṇerācārya) has been performed and that purpose has been completed,
there is the state of having become a preceptor— that is, the fact of its having arisen. Therefore,
it should be understood that once the initiations and so forth have been performed, these offices of preceptor have attained the state of having arisen.
In what sense does he also possess the status of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*)?
He states that when the purpose for which one is a preceptor has been accomplished, the state of having become [a disciple] arises:
(27) "When the preceptor has accepted the request, there is the arising of that [status]."
The manifestation of the status of preceptor (*upādhyāya*) occurs at the time of the request, when there is an acceptance by the preceptor;
it does not occur upon the formal going-forth (*pravrajyā*), the initiation (*upanayana*), or when the purpose characterized as full ordination (*upasaṃpanna*) has been accomplished.
For it is through that specific purpose being fulfilled that these states of teacherhood and preceptorship arise.
Regarding when that meaning comes to be accomplished, he says:
(28) "Upon the completion of the third limb, there is the state of being accomplished at the end."
That object in which there is a recurrence is the referent;

that aspect of it, such as teacherhood and so forth, by which its state of being repeated is constituted is the "repetition" (āvṛtti). In that [repetition], there is the state of being repeated belonging to the object.
And those revolutions are threefold;
therein it is not known in which revolution, or in which part of a revolution [this occurs].
To this, it is said: therein, in the last, the final one.
When it recurs, one should consider that the object has occurred within its third part.
He explains this matter by means of an illustration: (29) for example, at the time of proclaiming the praises of another, [one does not speak of] one's own status as a śrāmaṇera.
At the time of proclaiming another as the preceptor (*upanetṛ*),

and after the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) has been designated, when there is the proclamation of another as "preceptor" (*ācārya*), therein lies the meaning of the preceptor which constitutes the state of a novice, namely that which is called the novice restraint (*śrāmaṇerasaṃvara*).
Its status as a formal procedure (vṛtta) should be understood;
in this case, it should be understood that one says, "May the teacher uphold it," and not, "May the Venerable One uphold it."
(30) Regarding the phrase "in this [case] of the status of preceptor" (*upādhyāyatva*) in the latter [part],
the term "being established in conduct" (*vṛttatva*) is understood to carry over.

In this context, during the time of proclaiming others, following the request for many preceptors (*upādhyāya*) with the words "pay heed" (*asamanvāhara*) and the proclamation of the connection to the *bhikṣu* community, there follow the proclamations of the preceptors.
Among those, regarding the third proclamation— "I shall go forth under a preceptor" or "I shall receive full ordination"—
it refers to the fact that one's own status has already been established through the prior acceptance of the purpose of being a preceptor at that time.
At that very time, it should be said by the preceptor regarding the going forth (*pravrajyā*) and also regarding the full ordination (*upasaṃpad*):
"If he has not already been a preceptor previously," [then he must become one].
Nor by the teacher,
nor by the venerable one;
and here, the third part should be understood as being from the perspective of non-interruption.
It is not by the number of syllables;
for in this way, there are three formal requests when requesting a preceptor: "I, named so-and-so, request the Venerable One as my preceptor," and "[Venerable One], may you be my preceptor."
"Venerable Upādhyāya, I shall go forth;
I shall receive full ordination."
However, regarding the attainment of the state of a *śrāmaṇera*, there are two interruptions: the going for refuge and the formal acceptance of the *śrāmaṇera* status.

Therein, the latter interruption is divided into two parts according to the sequence of intermediate meanings—namely, "May I be a *śrāmaṇera*" and "May the Preceptor hold me [as such]"—and thus the triad is established.

Why, then, does the status of being a limb [of the Saṃgha] occur in the third [ordination] even though the procedure (*āvr̥tti*) is not yet completed? It is because it has been performed "for the most part" (*yadbhūyaḥ*). Furthermore, this rule regarding the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) and so forth should be understood as applying to all [stages]. Thus, while the private instruction (*raho'nuśāsana*) by the instructor (*raho'nuśāsaka*) is not yet finished, the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) belongs to the one who initiates the novicehood (*śrāmaṇeratvopanāyin*); at this time, the ritual agent (*karmakāraka*) acts in such a manner. This concludes the matter.
It is not known when [the offense occurs] for the provider of support and the reciter,
because the duration of the provision of support and the recitation is not fixed.
In this regard, that which constitutes the state of being a teacher for these two is explained as follows:
(31) The limit of providing dependence (*niḥśraya*) is to present oneself as a point of reliance for one night.
"One night" means one day and night; thus, it is "for one night."
The limit of providing dependence is precisely that presence as a support for one who is dependent upon a preceptor of dependence (*niśrayācārya*).
And thus says the text: "Who is the preceptor of dependence?"
"In whose presence he has stayed for even a single night by way of dependence"—
from this point onward, his [status] attains its complete form.
That which is merely touched upon, not yet reached its limit, and remains latent in the mind as something unaccomplished, cannot be counted among the certainties.
(32) Reciting the text by alternating three verses at a time.
The one from whom three single verses have been recited with the intention of study is the *pāṭhācārya* (recitation teacher).
For such is the limit of recitation.
And thus says the text: "Who is the *pāṭhācārya*?"
"From whomsoever one has returned, even two verses having been recited three times are mastered"—
this is the intended meaning of the scriptural text (*ārṣagrantha*) observed here.
*Udgraha* is the recitation by a student of what has been spoken by the teacher of the text.
When [the text] is spoken only once, the reading—being merely a touch and incomplete in form—is retained in the mind;
however, from the third repetition onwards, a continuous sequence is perceived as if it were already mastered.
Therefore, this reading up to that point is the correct one.
But the master Ratnasiṃha said: "The readings are exactly of this kind; it was upon seeing these that he composed this sūtra."
But this is logical,
because he formulates the sūtra independently of that treatise.
In that regard, he explains the origin [of the text]:
however, this has been composed as a mere sūtra without logical argumentation; it must necessarily have been of such a nature here, being the word of the Sage (ārṣa).
(33) Recitation does not consist in utterance with the intention of not reciting. Any utterance made with the intention of not reciting—
for example, that which occurs in a recitation class and the like— is not considered recitation at all.
Because this conventional usage is well-established in the sense of practicing recitation,
the status of being a teacher does not arise from this.
(34) One should not present these two in any other way.
These two— the *ācārya* and the *upādhyāya*—
are titles (*upapada*).
They should not be used as titles preceded by such honorifics as "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*), "Worthy One" (*bhadanta*), or "Elder" (*sthavira*).

However, the mention of "without an adjunct" (*nirupapada*) in the case of these two [names] should be understood as already prohibited by the rule: "One should not utter the name of an elder without an adjunct."
The teacher (ācārya) should be addressed simply as "teacher" (ācārya),
and the preceptor (upādhyāya) as "preceptor" (upādhyāya).
(35) "It is not thus, nor otherwise."
A person other than the preceptor (ācārya) or the instructor (upādhyāya) should not be designated by the terms "preceptor" or "instructor."
(36) Without first stating, "I shall not mention [your] name for the sake of gain," one should not utter the name of one's preceptor.
"Accompanied" means that one should utter the preceptor's name together with the sentence, "I mention the name for the sake of the purpose," meaning that one should not omit this phrase.

And that [act] is the immediate cause for this, wherein there arises the understanding: "This person has desisted from activity. This is the procedure for the ordination into the state of a *śrāmaṇera*.
(ii) The Procedure for Ordination (37):
Ordination from the Saṃgha.
The going forth and the undertaking of the status of a śrāmaṇera do not come from an individual person, but rather full ordination comes from the Saṃgha.
(38) One who has set his face toward the office of preceptor should seek out a laborer and a monk who will provide private instruction.

"Intent upon the state of being a preceptor" means having presented himself as the preceptor for full ordination (*upasaṃpad*). "He should request" means he should make a formal petition; and "he should also request the one who provides private instruction."
The mention of "a monk" (*bhikṣu*) is for the purpose of designating the instructor in private, not for the purpose of designating the performer of the ritual action;
for the status of being a monk is already established for him by the very injunction regarding the ritual action that is stated in the section on the definition of the ritual action itself.
(39) He should request a preceptor;
thus, having been ordained, he [should do so] in the midst of the Saṃgha.
(40) He himself should cause him to take formal possession of these three robes.
The word "he" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
The word "himself" means that there is no allowance for another person here— as there is in the case of shaving the head and so forth— but rather that he must perform this himself.
"Enam" refers to the one who is to be ordained.
If possible,
one should have him [adhiṣṭhāpayet] repair what is torn or frayed.
If it does not exist, one should understand that it is something other than the category of robes.
Because they serve the purpose of dress, it should be understood that these are worn immediately after the formal empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna).
(41) Having displayed the bowl, one should maintain silence; [the bowl] is superior if it is white or pale.
Thus [it is said] regarding the Saṃgha.
The word "having shown" (upadarśya) is connected with the word "in the Saṃgha" (saṃghe).
He asks, "For what purpose is the demonstration? and says: "It is for the sake of avoiding the fault that [the robe] is excessively white";
for it is improper to authorize such a thing.
The phrase "having demonstrated it, one should authorize it before the Saṃgha" follows as a continuation.
(42) "He is a worthy recipient," they should all say, provided he is not otherwise.
Thus, the monks who have assembled are of such a nature, of such a state;
they are possessed of defects such as deficiency and the like.
"Not thus" and "not not thus" means being free from these faults.
(43) When he has departed, the community, having announced who the instructor in private is and having encouraged him, should obtain his authorization for this person.
"Removed" means that the candidate for full ordination has been led away from the site of the mandala to another place;
since the ritual performed by the private instructor is not heard [by others], "removal" here has the sense of leading away.
No other [direction] is seen;
therefore, one should proceed according to the rule of action toward that place where, while standing, this hearing does not reach him.
It will be stated further on: "In the context of the preliminary examination (*darśanopavicāra*), they should have him stand facing the assembly with palms joined in reverence.

Regarding the phrase "having had him declare who [he is]": he is asked, "By whom were you requested? and he declares the private instructor (*rahonuśāsaka*) by name, using this formula: "I am so-and-so; such-and-such a person is my private instructor.
Regarding the phrase "having encouraged him": [he says], "You yourself are the private instructor."
With the words "Are you able? and so forth, one should obtain the permission of this instructor of secret teachings;
for this purpose, the officiant (karmakāraka) should perform the formal motion (jñapti).

Some read this mantra as "the Saṃgha should appoint such-and-such a person as the private instructor," but that is incorrect; for it would entail that the formal ritual proclamation (karmavācanā) must also be performed, yet there is no basis for such a requirement here.
This is not a formal agreement, but rather a request for permission;
such is the established rule. Therefore, when it is said, "Let the preceptor named so-and-so instruct the one named so-and-so in private," this is appropriate in the context of granting permission.
The formal authorization (*anujñāpana*) is thus formulated in the Sūtra, not the consent (*saṃmati*).
One should instruct [the candidate] in private, saying: "Listen to you! (44).
The term "instructor in private" (raho'nuśāsaka) is to be understood by implication.
"Listen, O Venerable One;
this is your time for truth"— in such a mantra, there is an indication by the phrase "listen,
you," [followed by] "stand" or "do not."
Having been addressed with "You shall come when called," he was thus instructed.
(45) "Instructed" means having reported one's purity to the Saṃgha.
Such is the established rule.
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen: this person named [so-and-so], instructed by me with such-and-such a mantra, etc.—should he come? Thus one should ask regarding his arrival.
Thus is the Saṃgha.
(46) If they should all say, "He is pure," [then he is so].
Thus [are] the monks who confer full ordination.
Some here and in the previous section recite a response to the announcement for the sake of going forth: "The entire Saṃgha should say, 'If he is pure';
he [the candidate] should say, 'I am pure'. That is untenable;
it is merely placing a burden upon the speaker.
Because it was explained by the instructor of the retreat right at the very beginning.
(47) The officiant of the ritual should request full ordination.
One who seeks full ordination.
(48) Having obtained permission from the Saṃgha, he should inquire about the obstructing factors.
Having made a formal motion for the purpose of inquiring about obstacles:
"Listen, venerable one;
this is the time for you to speak the truth."
The inquiry regarding obstacles is performed with the mantra beginning, "This is your past time," and so forth.
(49) He should confer full ordination.
By means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations.
The agent who performs the action at the appropriate occasion.

(50) "One should inform [the candidate] of the shadow immediately after the ordination. This means that immediately after the ordination (*upasaṃpad*) and the initiation (*upanayana*), one should inform the ordained person of the shadow. "Immediately" (*anantaram*) means without delay.

He explains how one should measure: since there is no possibility of breaking the posture for one who has remaining tasks, this measurement is joined with something other than the agent of the action.
Furthermore, he asks by what means this measurement of his feet and so forth is made, and says: (51) "By means of a peg four *aṅgulas* long; this is correct."
This measurement is for the sake of avoiding excessive length; a measurement of four finger-breadths is auspicious.
(52) It is designated as "person" (puruṣa) by way of conventional usage.
The word "sādhu" (good/so be it) continues [from the previous context].
Regarding the phrase "of this," it refers to the four-finger-width peg;
the meaning is that one should state the shadow of the person (pauruṣī-chāyā) to be as many times the length of the pegs as there are pegs.

(53) "One should know the divisions of the day and night, such as the forenoon and so forth"— this [phrase] continues [from the previous rule]. This is stated in the text beginning with "forenoon, midday," and so on.
(54) And the agreement: "These five."
One should know these five as the seasonal observances (*samaya*): the winter [retreat], and so forth. (55) *Haimantika*.
The summer, the rainy season, and the limited rainy season.
"One who has spent the long rainy season retreat."
Their duration is stated as follows: (56) the first two last for four months each;
[the remaining two] are the winter and summer [retreats].
(57) At most one month; thus [is] the rainy-season [retreat].
(58) "Then, a day-and-night":
following that [rainy-season month], one day-and-night consists of a Mitavārṣika [month] plus [one additional day].
(59) "Deficient by that; the final three months":
deficient by that single day and night, the final period consists of three months, which is the long rainy season.
Immediately after the ordination ceremony is concluded,
the officiant of the ritual should inform [the candidate] of the dependencies (*niḥśraya*).
Those four, beginning with the refuse-rag robe (pāṃsukūla), are [the ascetic practices].
(61) The offenses involving defeat, the *pārājika* dharmas.
And one should announce the "maker-of-a-śramaṇa" [precepts], such as "when reviled, one should not revile in return," and so forth; the word "one should announce" continues to apply here.
Having grasped the perfection and correctness of that which is desired, one should engage them in delighting in the commonality of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
"Prepsita" means intensely desired, sought after, or intended.
That which was previously his aspiration, such as "May I obtain [this]," and so forth—this is what he longed for. Having perceived that this [longing] of his has been fulfilled, the sentient being...

By the passage beginning "now, one who has gone forth and received full ordination," etc., the state of being "right" (samyaktā) is further described by means of a suitable preceptor (upādhyāya), etc. Having grasped the state of being "accomplished" (saṃpannatā), he says what should be done: "One should engage [the disciple] in the attainment of commonality in moral discipline (śīla-sāmānyagatatā)."
In this context, by the phrase "with one ordained for a hundred years" and so forth, "commonality of morality" (*sāmānyagatatā*) refers to the state of having attained equality in morality;
its "gratification" (*ārāgaṇa*) means its fulfillment.
(64) One should employ [the mind] in the reflection of the connection with the objective support (*ālambana*).
This is to be understood as applicable in all cases.

The relationship of the alms-bowl is the relationship of mother and father; its reflection is [to be cultivated] by means of the thought, "From this day forward, you shall regard your preceptor as your mother and father," and so forth. In this way, that relationship with householders, having been practiced by you, is to be reflected upon.
(65) Regarding dwelling in harmony with those who are disciplined:
"From this day forward, you must act with reverence," and so forth.
(66) In the performance of the purpose.

"From this day forward, you must teach [the precepts]," and so forth; he should explain to one who has already completed his full understanding of what has been undertaken that which is currently being undertaken and has not yet been declared.
And by means of these and those most gross [faults], and so forth,
there will now come about the full comprehension of that which has been undertaken and practiced without having been previously explained. (VinSū 13)
(68) One should apply oneself with diligence.

By means of the two verses beginning with "Thus you have attained ordination" and the verse beginning with "Of one who has reached this," he demonstrates the difficulty of obtaining the perfection of the opportune moment (*kṣaṇasampad*).

For even when other non-opportune states (*akṣaṇa*) are absent, and even when human birth— which is obtained through the compassion of others— is achieved along with the possession of right view, there are many obstacles here consisting of various forms of impurity and deformity.
Therefore, this is difficult to obtain.
(69) And the narration of the means [is required] for the accomplishment [of the goal].
Along with the explanation of the means, there is the explanation of the means itself;
he should enjoin him to accomplish that for which he has gone forth and received full ordination— by saying, "Venerable one, having been ordained, accomplish [your goal] through heedfulness"—
just as, for example, "you have attained this state."
"Now one must take delight in this.

First, regarding the formalities (*sāmīcī*): there are three acts of prostration toward the assembled Saṃgha during the instruction; then, while seated in the *utkuṭuka* posture before the instructor, [one performs them]. During the private instruction, [the candidate] stands for the full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), having placed the alms-bowl in his left hand.
Since the passage beginning with "having covered [it] with the right hand" will be explained later in the section on the ritual object (*karmavastu*), it is not included here.
The procedure for full ordination.
(iii) Regarding dependence (70): one should not perform what is to be done by one who is dependent without first looking to the one upon whom one depends.
"Not asking" means not looking; the meaning is that one should do nothing without having asked.

The Blessed One has stated that for one who is intent on observing what must be done, even if there is something to be done, it may be performed without asking permission; thus he said: (71) "Except for the evacuation of excrement and urine, the discarding of the tooth-stick, and the salutation of the monastery, its precincts, and the caityas."
That which is pervaded by internal activities such as threshing and the like is the courtyard of the shrine (*caityāṅgana*);
it is appropriate that this be considered an "accessory" (*upavicāra*) here.
Together with the accessory is "with-accessory" (*sopavicāra*).
And therein lies a shrine;
its salutation [is performed].
(72) Departing from a monastery that extends for forty-nine vyāmas.
The word "muktvā" (having released) is the grammatical connection (*anubandha*).
"Ekānnapañcāśat" (forty-nine) is a *āṭa*-sandhi formation; the meaning is "up to the limit of forty-nine fathoms (*vyāma*)."
In a monastery where there is a moat, a wall, or some other enclosure, it is appropriate to determine that its limit is at that [enclosure].
When there are multiple walls and so forth, the outermost one is the limit.
Therefore, in that case, the outer side of this measurement is its limit;
however, where there is no secondary chamber (*upavicāra*), the monastery wall itself is the limit. That which lies beyond it is the location of the previously mentioned secondary chamber.
And the shrine located therein is not to be saluted;
thus it is established here.
This is the authorization for one who has become subject to wandering.
Furthermore, regarding the matter of paying homage to a *caitya*, what should be understood in this regard?
One should not go there for that purpose without having asked permission;
however, once one has gone for the sake of wandering about, one should pay homage.

This object to be accomplished is twofold: that which consists of an undertaking and that which consists of a natural inclination. Among these, there is a prohibition only of that which consists of an undertaking; however, for that which consists of a natural inclination, its non-prohibitability is established.
One should not address them without having first asked for permission,
nor converse with them, nor exchange greetings.
One should not give a reply;
nor should one wipe the feet, the face, the heart, or other parts of the body with a hand moistened with water; nor should there be wiping of the hands and so forth with water.
Because of the occurrence of such behavior as "clothes and so forth covered with dust must be shaken out," which serves as a basis for laughter.

(VinSū 14) Regarding the mention of sandals, tooth-sticks, and recitation—since these refer to the performance and the conclusion of private study, and because of the specific inclusion of "from a monk of that same class," it is understood that what is intended here is one who has become submissive. In this context, a renunciant who is known to be wicked or suspected is not to be abandoned unless he has been questioned; no other [is so].

For there is no cognition of the performance [of the ritual] as being characterized by the act of reciting, or performing private study (*svādhyāya*), or performing the concluding rites at the appropriate time for them, and so forth.
For its dwelling in the mind occurs by way of the manner of bowing down;
however, when [the mind] is corrupted, this very thing, appearing as a semblance while following after opposing factors, attains renown as an undertaking.
Therefore, the intended meaning seen here is that effort must be exerted in that regard.
The failure to seek permission regarding the drinking of water should be understood as having been committed through this very consideration;
for such is the case, just like the touching of Dharmila’s limbs with water.
The conduct based on reliance is said to be: [the conduct] regarding the work of the bowl and robes, and the nursing of the sick; (73)
He should apply intense eagerness toward the dispelling of remorse and the relinquishing of evil views, thinking: "O, would that I might do it, or cause it to be done!"
Some also recite "dyeing" here;
however, it is included because it does not exceed the category of robe-making.

(74) When the Saṃgha desires to perform a formal act of resolution—desiring to carry out a formal act of resolution such as the act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya*) and so forth—one should say to the Saṃgha: "O, may the Saṃgha not perform this formal act of resolution regarding this reliance!"
Thus he falls into intense longing and turns back—
this [process] should be understood as following throughout until [the hair] is plucked out.
(75) Once it has been performed, he should cause [the water] to flow out.
When this act of formal proposal has been performed—thinking, "O, may the Saṃgha grant him absolution"—it is so.

(76) Regarding one who requests parivāsa, mūlaparivāsa, mānāpya, mūlamānāpya, or ābarhaṇa, the formal support (*niśraya*) is: "O, may the Saṃgha grant him the fourfold [penances] beginning with parivāsa"; and regarding one who requests ābarhaṇa, it is: "O, may he perform the ābarhaṇa."
He too would do this for him,
having abandoned all looking back.
That too is a support;
one should perform tasks such as those concerning the bowl and robes for this person who is dependent on it.
Having abandoned all observation, with the exception of a single observation.
(78) One who is less than twenty years of age shall not perform the ordination, nor act as a preceptor, nor provide dependence, nor dwell independently.
One who has received full ordination but is less than ten years of age should not perform these three things.
(79) Even one who is less than ten years old may receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), provided there is no lack of [the required] equipment due to the combination of the preceding factors.
The meaning is that one who is endowed with even just one of those fivefold conjunctions (samāyoga) which will be explained immediately below is qualified [and no other].

And thus, regarding what was stated—that one must be "endowed with another five dharmas as well"—it should not be understood as a logical conjunction (samuccaya), such that one must possess both these and those others;
rather, it is said that at least these [five] must be performed.
"By these others as well"—this is the alternative.
Why is this so?
Because it is impossible for all these groups of five to provide testimony.

In the first *pañcikā*, however, when it is stated that "one who has ten years [of standing] is fit for the limbs" and "one who has ten years attains full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*)," this mention of "ten years" at the beginning is for the purpose of making known that this constitutes the scope for all subsequent [rules]. This is because the meaning is established in the Vinaya.
When one has reached the age of ten, this serves as the cause for the formal ordination (upādhyākaraṇa) and so forth.
If there exists a state of being distinguished therein for the remainder [of the requirements], it is "with distinction" (saviśeṣatva), which is the superior method;
if not, then even this much alone should be relied upon here.
Just as the specific qualities such as being a *śaikṣa* are to be bypassed, so too is this [quality] bypassed when one has reached ten years of age and is established in the meaning of the Vinaya.
Now, these combinations (*samāyoga*) are stated:

(80) the capacity for performing or causing others to perform the nursing of the sick, the dispelling of remorse, the relinquishing of evil views, and the closing down of the state of dissatisfaction.
By the inclusion of "the capacity for the removal of remorse," there is the demonstration of being established in the Vinaya;
by the inclusion of "the relinquishing of views," there is the demonstration of skillfulness in the stability of the Dharma;
and by the inclusion of "lack of delight, instability, and lethargy," there is the demonstration of being fit for application or having speech that is worthy of acceptance.
One should not think here that by the mention of "cause" (kāraṇa), an action was performed even by one who is incapable;
rather, it refers to the state of having acquired the capacity for engagement in activity toward others, provided that [the meaning] is accessible through the power of those to be trained (vineya).
And thus, in this case, there is the non-transgression of that cause which must not be transgressed—the state of being established in meaning within the Vinaya.
(81) Prior to the state of being a learner (*śaikṣa*), in the stage of the five aggregates, there is possession of ethical discipline (*śīlavattā*) and great learning (*bāhuśrutya*).
Prior to the states of being a learner (*śaikṣatva*) and being beyond learning (*aśaikṣatā*), that which was mentioned as a pentad does not exist.

For example: other combinations [of qualities] distinct from the combination of faith, ethical discipline, and so forth, should be understood as being accompanied by both possession of ethical discipline (*śīlavattā*) and great learning (*bāhuśrutya*).
Together with possession of ethical discipline and great learning, there is the pentad consisting of possession of ethical discipline and great learning.
In this regard, because of her possession of virtuous conduct, she is distinguished precisely by the impossibility of cohabiting with one who is immoral;
thus it should be understood that she is regarded as "this person is excellent."
Furthermore, regarding erudition (*bāhuśrutya*): in whatever application the mastery of the *piṭakas* is found, therein [it serves] against the opposing doctrines of others,
as well as against [the deficiencies in] the constituent parts such as the subject matter (*vastu*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*).
Where expertise in metrics (chandoviciti) and so forth, or in historical narratives (itihāsa-vṛttaka), is not found, there the inclusion of the Piṭakas should be understood.
(82) Mastery of the Piṭakas.
By adding mastery of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mātṛkās, as well as ethical conduct and great learning, there is a group of five;
it is stated in the Vinaya: "One who upholds the Sūtras..."
One who upholds the Vinaya,
one who upholds the Mātrikās,
and one who is proficient in the Sūtras.
He is proficient in the Vinaya, proficient in the Mātṛkā, and skilled in the Sūtras.
Skilled in the Vinaya, skilled in the Mātrikās, and proficient in the Sūtras.
"Expert in the Vinaya,
expert in the Mātṛkās. In this context, the non-forgetting of what has been grasped is the retention of the Sūtras and so forth.
And this is found within the Three Baskets (piṭakatraya).
Because one who has gone to one place perceives the other, [the dharmas] exist in a state of intermixture;
the capacity to discern this which exists in such a state is skill (*kauśala*).
The application of the *sūtras* and so forth through both reasoning and scripture is expertise (*kovidatva*).
Thus, when so applied, that capacity for communicating to another is what constitutes "manifestness" (vyaktatva).
All this, together with non-forgetfulness, is called "superknowledge" (*abhijñā*) by means of the general term "superknowledge."
(83) Their capacity [to act] is due to grasping.
One who is not proficient in the Piṭakas is not capable of grasping them;
therefore, this statement regarding proficiency in the Piṭakas should be understood as referring to a specific distinction.
(84) It consists in training in higher ethics, mind, and wisdom.
The state of being one who trains is "śikṣadbhāvaḥ";
it is a dual compound treated as a singular.

By the inclusion of "higher training in ethical discipline" (adhiśīla), there is the inclusion of the entire conduct of the Vinaya; by the inclusion of "higher training in mind" (adhicitta), there is the inclusion of the meditative absorptions (dhyānas);
and by the inclusion of "higher training in wisdom" (adhiprajñā), there is the inclusion of the cultivation of the vision of the truths.
(85) Or it is the capacity for training.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the phrase "with regard to higher morality, etc. for the purpose of generating confidence, not for the purpose of expressing an alternative;
for one who has not been trained in higher morality and so forth is not capable of training therein.
It should be understood that this expression "training" (śikṣā) refers specifically to the distinction itself.
(86) Thus [is] the Prātimokṣa as the discipline of higher conduct (*adhyācāravinaya*).
By the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), [it refers to] the state of being trained (*śikṣattā*) or the capacity for training (*śikṣaṇāyāṃ pratibalatvam*). (VinSū 16)
Adherence.
And thus, there are these two combinations:
therein, higher conduct (*adhyācāra*) consists of the rules of customary behavior (*āsamudācārika*), while discipline (*vinaya*) constitutes the remainder.
The *prātimokṣa* is that which consists of the training in the *prātimokṣa*, as well as the categories of subject matter along with their ancillaries;
the training precepts are included therein.
(87) The perfection of faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, and wisdom.
By the mention of "morality" (śīla) here, the Vinaya is included.
(88) By means of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision thereof.
"Endowment" (saṃpannatva) is the connection [to the term].
By the inclusion of the phrase "endowed with ethical discipline" (śīlasaṃpanna), it is implied here that [the subject] is characterized by the Vinaya,
and not otherwise.
Regarding the statement "the arising of a monk’s perfection of ethical discipline":
in the phrase "knowledge of that," the word "that" refers to liberation; thus, it means the knowledge and vision of liberation.
(89) And the state of having initiated vigor and being wise.

Prior to the state of being a learner (*śaikṣatva*), there is the presence of ethical discipline (*śīlavattā*) and extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*); by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), their simultaneous presence is indicated.

From this point upward, prior to the state of being a learner, that which was previously mentioned as a pentad (*pañcaka*) no longer applies; rather, it should be understood as being mentioned together with vigor (*vīryatva*) and wisdom (*prājñatva*).
Furthermore, here three [qualities] are stated individually along with ethical discipline and extensive learning—(90–92).
Possession of mindfulness.
The state of being withdrawn in solitary retreat.
The state of being concentrated.
Thus.
The fulfillment of these four qualities for them is as follows: he is virtuous, possessed of great learning, energetic, wise, and mindful.
Having stated this tetrad, it should further be said: "and he becomes withdrawn in meditative seclusion," and again, "he is concentrated."

(93) Regarding "the state of being a learner" (*śaikṣatva*): it is the possession of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of a learner, as well as the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of a learner; this is its summary.
(94) The state of one beyond training.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of the aggregate of morality of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣeṇa śīlaskandhena*), that thorough knowledge of what is proper and improper concerning the conduct determined by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) for these two is, first of all, derived from realization (*ādhigamika*). Furthermore, there is the thorough knowledge of the formal determination of offenses (*āpatti-vyavasthā*) and of the remaining rules of discipline (*vinaya-vidhi*).

In this case as well, because these two have been independent for ten years and more, they have certainly exerted effort; therefore, it should be understood that no transgression has been committed here due to a cause that ought not to be disregarded.
(95) Mastery over arising, designation, subsequent designation, rejection, and permission.
Therefore, this is designated by the word "origin" (*utpatti*) in the context of the origin of the training rules (*śikṣāpada-utpatti-nidāna*), meaning that it has arisen from this.
The formal establishment of the training rules is the "prescription" (*prajñapti*).

By the inclusion of the term "prescription," there is the inclusion of such passages as, "By this much [of an offense], one must confess a gross transgression (*sthūlātyaya*) in the presence [of another]."
Furthermore, in this context, there is the "subsequent designation" (*anuprajñapti*), which consists of what is prohibited and what is permitted.
For example, by the permission of shoes, there is the prohibition of specific qualities such as the sound "saṇ-saṇ.
And while eating at improper times is prohibited, there is permission for one who is ill, based on the word of a physician.
A prohibition is an injunction stating that "this must absolutely not be done," such as drinking even a drop of alcohol from the tip of a blade of grass, unchaste conduct, and so forth.
Permission, on the other hand, refers to an action for which there is no fault in either performing it or not performing it; here, one may proceed according to one's own will.
For example: "External treatises should be studied for the purpose of refuting opponents," and so forth.
In this regard, there is no fault of transgression whether one does not perform them or performs them.
This much should be understood as the thorough knowledge of what is to be done and what is not to be done within the Prātimokṣa-vinaya.
Thus, this state of being unacquainted with discipline should be understood as being further illustrated by two sets of five:
the five beginning with offenses, and so forth.
(96) The state of being one who has supernormal knowledge regarding what constitutes an obstacle and what does not constitute an obstacle, and the state of not being a teacher [of others].

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: it consists of being an expert in what constitutes an obstacle and what does not constitute an obstacle, being one who makes [these matters] known, and being an instructor. That which is not to be done according to the Vinaya is "an obstacle" (*āntarāyika*).
That which is to be done without obstruction consists of these two: mastery over the Vinaya and the state of being established in its meaning; this pair is what brings them forth.
Furthermore, "having made known" refers to the skillful capacity or the lack of indolence to speak or to awaken others to this very pair.
The quality of being an instructor (*anuśāsakatva*) consists in speaking in a manner appropriate for establishing [others] when they transgress,
and in being an expounder (*ācakṣaka*) in a manner appropriate for turning [them away] from indolence;
thus has the meaning of this very reading, "instructor" (*anuśāsaka*), been explained.

Some read "instructs" (*avavadati*) and "admonishes" (*anuśāsti*) in place of these two. Therein, "admonishes" is equivalent to being an admonisher; by this [term], it is meant that one acts as a teacher.
"Instructs" is the designation for that instruction which is for the purpose of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
For this purpose is the going forth;
therefore, he especially deserves this here,
namely, the gathering of the assembly, or rather, his inclusion within it.
(97) Together with the capacity for grasping, there is that of the reliance or the secondary reliance.
The capacity for grasping and the excessive capacity for grasping—
along with this capacity for grasping, there is this pentad beginning with the state of being an obstructor to that [grasping] and the superknowledges (abhijñā).
There are these two combinations: one is that which pertains to dependence (*niśraya*), having added [the fourth] to this group of four;
the other is that which pertains to proximity (*upaniśraya*). The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of demonstrating this.
When the preceptor departs elsewhere, one's capability in receiving formal dependence (*niśraya*) is required; that is,

when the preceptor or another person of dependence departs with the intention of returning for a limited time, and due to the influence of certain people, one remains [in that place], one's capability in receiving temporary dependence (*upaniśraya*) is required.
It is employed.
(98) The detailed exposition of the Prātimokṣa, which consists in the knowledge of what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the gravity or lightness of those offenses.

In that regard, the application of expertise concerning what constitutes an offense and what does not consists in relying on the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done; and the application of expertise concerning the gravity or lightness [of an offense] consists in the confession of gross transgressions.
By the phrase "the detailed exposition of the Prātimokṣa," it is shown that the Vinaya possesses its intended meaning (*adhiṣṭhitārthatva*).

And by this word "detailed exposition" (*vistara*), the Vinaya itself is understood. Furthermore, one should not think that the term "detailed exposition of the Prātimokṣa" does not refer to the *Vibhaṅga* along with the remainder of the text, such as the *Vastu*, the *Kṣudraka*, and so forth.

Because this [text] constitutes the detailed exposition of the entire Prātimokṣa, there is an "arising" from the very beginning of the Prātimokṣa; specifically, the arising from the section on Ordination (*pravrajyāvastu*) begins with the words: "Furthermore, [the case] of a monk together with nuns."
"O Venerable Ones, the *poṣadha*" refers to the *Poṣadha-vastu*; "the special *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and those who have not yet completed their year" refers to the *Varṣika-vastu*.
For this very reason, the *Pravāraṇā-vastu* is established in connection with the rainy-season residence (*varṣāvāsa*).
"‘When the kaṭhina has been lifted’" refers to the matter of the *kaṭhina*; "‘by a monk whose robe is finished’" refers to the matter of the robe (*cīvara*).
"The category of robes and the category of leather and medicine" refers to the matter of leather, precisely because of the causes for its arising.
"Those medicines which were permitted by the Blessed One for sick monks"—this is from the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*.
"Announce the consent (*chanda*) and the purity (*pariśuddhi*) of those venerable ones who have not yet arrived;
do not strive to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha"—this is from the beginning of the *Kauśāmbikavastu* and the *Saṃghabhedavastu*.
And for this reason, from the *Pravrajyāvastu* and other sections indicating such acts, there is the rule regarding "non-attainment" (*alābha*); and here too,
from the *Karmavastu* beginning with "by him," and from the *Pāṇḍulohitavastu* beginning with "that monk must undergo a period of probation (*parivāsa*) within the Saṅgha."
Because of the absence of intentional intent regarding the matter of the probationary period (*parivāsa*) through actions and so forth,
there is the subsequent formal determination of the offense, its confession, and the acknowledgment before the *saṃgha*;
therefore, this concerns the matter of the suspension of the *poṣadha*.
By the phrase "the great monastery of the bhikṣus," the matter of bedding and seating is indicated;

furthermore, by the establishment of the *āpatti* (offenses) and the *poṣadha* (confessional ceremony), the matter of legal procedures (*adhikaraṇa*) is demonstrated for the sake of showing its functional capacity.
That which constitutes a factor of speech is of the same nature as other [factors] such as conduct (*śīlacāra*).

The Prātimokṣa is twofold: the [rules concerning] the primary matters and the remainder. The explanation of the minor rules and the matters contained in the Mātṛkā, as well as the exposition of such things, constitutes the *pṛcchā* (interrogation).
Furthermore, the exposition of conduct consists of the *pṛcchā* and the *vinītaka-rāṇi* (supplementary disciplinary rules).
Items such as hides and so forth [are permitted] for children;
for in that case, this detailed exposition of the Prātimokṣa does not remain exhaustive.
When one proceeds by means of the Vibhaṅga alone, the undertaking of going forth and other such acts does not take place.
The same applies to those things that ought to be done, because this [text] merely demonstrates a representative selection thereof.
(99) In the absence of elders, one should rely on novices.
If an elder monk were not endowed with even some semblance of the five [qualities], then this is the rule: "Venerable sir, this monk has fewer than sixty years since his full ordination;
he has extensively mastered, recited, and [retained] the Prātimokṣasūtra."
It does not happen because of that,
Upāli, unless he has departed elsewhere.
It has been stated that one must rely upon another.

In this regard, even a sixty-year-old who is not independent (*asvatantra*)— that is, dependent (*niśrita*)— is described by the phrase "in the absence of growth" and so forth, because there is no distinction in his extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*).
(100) With the sole exception of the formal salutation (*sāmīci*):
thus, in this case, the act of veneration is not included within the precepts and vows,
except when a junior [monk] relies upon an elder.
The intended meaning is that he should be made to dwell together [with them].
(101) One who has completed five years of training, being independent and endowed with the final conjunction, may wander through the countryside.
The final conjunction consists of [the knowledge of] offenses and non-offenses, and so forth;
endowed with that, one who has been ordained for five years and is independent should wander through the countryside.
(102) Otherwise, even one who possesses the threefold knowledge [would not be so].
Endowed with five qualities,
even one who is less than five years [of standing],
though he may have fallen from the path and from the discipline, becomes transformed through suffering by virtue of his union with the practice of the five-year precepts.
The underlying intention seen here is that one who has not yet completed a full year [of training] is not [yet qualified].

Regarding the phrase "even those possessing the three knowledges," there is a twofold thorough mastery of the training: the complete understanding of what is to be done and what is not to be done, based on the reliance upon the teacher and the meaning of that reliance.
In this regard, although his true nature (*dharmatā*) consists in direct knowledge (*abhijñā*),

because he acts through the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and possesses the perfection attained by practicing difficult and rare forms of awareness, he achieves a thorough understanding of what is to be done and what is not to be done.
In this way, for the sake of those to be trained, one should rely upon a support;
because, in order to discipline the conventional usage of suffering, there is the abandonment of the intrinsic nature of existence as previously associated with a self.
It is heard that for the Arhats, there is the abandonment of their previous intrinsic nature.
