A certain Arhat is a field of merit, one who has transcended all fields of merit;
he is the Venerable One. (VinSū 19)
Furthermore, Pilindavatsa addressed Gaṅgādevī as a "śūdrī," and so forth;
moreover, a thorough understanding of the Vinaya has not been achieved by anyone,
because of its extreme difficulty.
Just as a large man and a young girl cannot coexist on the same floor, so too there is an abundance of obstacles among various endeavors;
for this reason, this section is diverse.

[That is to say: Venerable Sir, if one who possesses the three knowledges (*traividya*) and has abandoned the three stains for three years were not endowed with five qualities, would he also, being independent, wander through the countryside?
"It is not so, Upāli," it was said.
And he must guard that which pertains to discipline;
he should distance himself from this [transgression] far, far away, for the sake of achieving the perfection of avoidance.
This is for the purpose of avoiding that conduct through which others might lose their confidence.
Even though he has accomplished his purpose, he trains himself with respect for this [teaching] in order to generate reverence and,
for the sake of the stability of the teaching, he proceeds by transgressing [ordinary] renown and so forth.
If there were some transgression, then the teaching would otherwise come to ruin;
therefore, just as there is no permission for anyone else in this matter, so it is for one who possesses the threefold knowledge.
Concerning the bases of reliance.

(iv) Regarding matters to be included: one who has approached for the sake of going forth should be asked, "Are you not a heretic? by both the ordaining preceptors and those performing the full ordination.

"He should ask" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). "They should ask" is connected with the phrase "the ordainers (*upasaṃpādaka*) of one who has reached maturity. That same question which is asked by the private instructor (*raho'nuśāsaka*) is [here] asked by the ordainers themselves.
Because he is appointed to that [task].

(104) They shall not cause anyone to go forth or confer full ordination upon a non-Buddhist ascetic, whether he be a Śākya, an Āgneya, or one with matted hair, unless his mind has been won over [by the Buddha].
Surely some similarity of intention was observed between the Śākya and the Agneya: "If these two were to act, their action would certainly be out of sincere conviction, not out of artifice."

Therefore, it should be understood that this was permitted: when the Blessed One said, "I grant an exemption for kinsmen," he perceived that these people would act toward one another as if they were not kin; thus, he spoke of granting an exemption on account of kinship.
In this context, it should be understood that one who has entered the fire-related practice through devotion—
that is, one abiding in the purification of that intention— is "taken up," because for such a person, a failure of intention is impossible.

This should be understood as having the designation "kṛt" (done), excluding the word "pūrvatīrthya" from the phrase beginning with "tīrthyānārādhitādi-tīrthyānta-varjam," and excluding the sequence starting with the word "anārādhita" and ending with the word "tīrthya" from the phrase "anārādhitacittam utsṛjya śākyaṃ āgneyaṃ ca jaṭilaṃ tīrthyaṃ," specifically that which was stated as "mā asi" and so forth.
Where it is said "it is not done," there one should ask the person who has approached for the sake of going forth, "Are you not [one of these]?
and the ordainers should neither let him go forth nor let him be ordained; this is how the uttered [injunction] is to be understood.
Regarding the "prescriptions concerning the *kṛt* suffixes," [this refers to] what follows here in this very section on ordination (*pravrajyā*) and within the *Kṣudrakavastu*.

To determine the extent to which a non-Buddhist (*tīrthya*) may be said to have a gratified mind, he says: (105) When one speaks truthfully of the praise of the Jewels and the dispraise of the non-Buddhists, his state of being unprovoked is his having a gratified mind.
That which does not become agitated is "unagitated" (*akupya*); the state of being unagitated is "unagitativeness" (*akupyatva*).

(VinSū 20) (106) For that purpose, the Saṃgha, having granted him probation through a formal act (*karma*), should cause this person—who does not possess those qualities but has completed the status of a lay follower—to undergo probation for four months.
‘For that purpose’ means for the purpose of propitiating the mind;
and ‘one who does not possess that’ means one whose mind is not propitiated.
The word "that" refers to the heretic.
"Having performed the final rite of the lay follower" means having completed the procedure for the status of a lay follower (*upāsakatānta*).

Thus, in that case, the Saṃgha, by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), shall grant and cause [the offender] to undergo the *parivāsa* probation for four months.
Regarding the granting of the *parivāsa* penance, he should receive his meal from the Saṃgha.
(108) A robe from one's preceptor.

(109) [The teacher] should inquire of one who has approached for the sake of going forth, [asking: "Is the agency regarding the undertaking of the task complete? and "(110) Are you fifteen years of age?"
The preceptor.
(111) If a nine-year-old is incapable of flying like a crow,
or even if he is capable, they may ordain him only after he has reached seven years [of age].
These two are not to be ordained: one who is incapable because he is less than fifteen years of age, and one who is capable because he is seven years of age.
For what purpose is the plural number used in the phrase "they should not ordain"?
It is so that the informant, having realized "this person is impure," should not report him.
The Saṃgha must not grant permission;
this is for the purpose of inclusion, namely that one who would lead another into the state of a śrāmaṇera must not lead them into the state of a śrāmaṇera [without authorization].
(112) One should not ordain a novice monk by oneself alone.

Since it follows that if one does not attend to a second candidate for the status of a śrāmaṇera, one also fails to ordain the second, he says— by way of an exception to that— the following: (113) "If there is no desire for the going forth repeatedly,
one should confer full ordination [upon him] once he has gone beyond the stage of the novice."

Having decided, "For the sake of going forth, we two must go forth together in one [place]," if there is a lack of unanimity— that is, a lack of desire for separate ordinations— then both should be ordained, and the one who exceeds the other [in seniority] should be fully admitted.
(114) If it is deficient, one should hand it over to another for the purpose of relying upon it.
If he is less than twenty years of age, he must be entrusted to another monk for the purpose of providing him with formal dependence (*upaniśraya*).
One to whom [an object] has been entrusted for the purpose of being used as a support should not take it back from him.
He by whom [the candidate] was presented should ordain him;
even if he does not offer [him], one should take him by force.
Since the gift is given for the sake of another by means of reliance,
and not out of a sense of having already surrendered it, therefore it is "inviolable."
(117) A slave by deed.

By this designation "kṛt," there arises the presentation of the designata— such as "amā" and "asi"— as being related to the servant. Therefore, whatever is accepted as additional in this context of designation and named [element],
even when transformed according to its actual meaning, settles in its proper place.
And this statement is understood here:
"One should ask one who has approached for the sake of going forth, 'Are you a slave?
And the ordainers [should neither ordain nor confer full ordination upon] a slave.
(118) If you have been requested by someone for anything whatsoever, whether it be little or much, [you should give it].
"Free from *asi*" means "devoid of the word *asi*"; that is to say, [the suffix] *kṛt* should be stated [as the substitute].
Furthermore, in place of "of *asi*," one should say "of *te*."

And then this statement: "Nothing whatsoever, whether little or much, should be given by you to anyone"—this [the teacher] should ask of one who has approached for the sake of going forth, and the ordainers [should also ask], because of the rule: "They should not cause one who is indebted to go forth or to receive full ordination."

Having released one who declares, "In this matter, I shall be able to take up the going-forth and full ordination," it should be understood that the specific qualification "one who is not indebted" applies.
(119) One who has living parents and has not been permitted by them, yet seeks ordination while remaining in their vicinity, should be kept for seven days.
"One who has living parents" refers to one whose father and mother are alive;
"by them" means by the mother and father.
From those two and from the word "mātā-pitroḥ," the term *pitṛ* [is understood] here.
(120) Even if it has not been announced, one should ordain this person into the Saṃgha, even if he is from a distant land.
"Enam" refers to one whose father is still living and who has received permission.
It should be understood that for one whose father is deceased, or for one who has been permitted by both parents, there is no fault even if he does not inform his mother and father.

Accordingly, the reading of the inquiry regarding one whose father is deceased is as follows: "Venerable sir, for one whose mother and father have passed away, or have gone to the state of animals—for the shaving of his hair, the entire Saṅgha..."
"No indeed, Upāli.
For what purpose was the inclusion of the phrase "distant region" made?
Because a certain householder’s wife whose son had gone forth into homelessness came and said: "You [should give this] to them..."
"Why have you gone forth among these thieves who are sons of the Śākyas?
Come, let us go! Having said this, she took hold of him and led him home.
Thus, in this case, the fault lies in the practice of theft itself;
it is not the case that this fault is absent when one is in a distant land, for even those staying in their own place incur the fault once they have heard [of the act] and committed it.
Furthermore, because the occurrence of harm is possible even after having arrived, it is therefore stated in the Sūtra: "even to a distant place."
(121) It is proper for the Saṃgha to provide a meal for one who desires to go forth into the religious life.
"It is logical" means that this is not a fixed rule;
he makes it known that those monks proceeded because they were not being observed.
(122) Have you been granted permission by your parents, except in the case of one who has gone to a distant land?
"Anujñato 'si" (you are permitted) is used in place of "mā asi";
at the end of what is spoken by this [phrase], one should understand that the word "dūradeśakaṃ" (to a distant place), excluding "kṛt," is added.
And thus, the sentence is: "anujñato 'si mātāpitṛbhyām" (you are permitted by your mother and father).

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of going forth' and so on, up to: 'they shall not ordain or grant full admission to one who has not been permitted by his parents, except in the case of one from a distant land.'"
(123) One should ask a person who has approached [for ordination], "Are you not ill? before granting full ordination.
It should be understood from the context that [the purpose] is for the sake of going forth.
(124) Or [the thought]: "Do you have any weariness at all?"
This is the connection regarding the alternative reading;
it shows that one or the other of the two must be stated.
(125) Specifically, those who confer full ordination.
Regarding the phrase "one should ask," the word "they should ask" is to be supplied as the subject of this transformed form. Indeed, such bodily afflictions as these occur in persons, namely:
leprosy, boils, and so forth, characterized by various specific ailments. It is not merely a matter of saying, "May you not be ill."
(126) They should not ordain or grant full admission to one who is ill.
The plural number is used because there is much activity on the part of many Saṃghas who perform the functions of announcing, ordaining, and admitting one to the state of a śrāmaṇera.
(127) [The term] *kṛt* [is used] prior to what has been previously resolved (*praṇihita*).
From the point "He has not accepted the reversal of signs or the wishless" until the end of the exposition, it should be understood that the term *kṛt* (the suffix -kṛt) is supplied everywhere;
all those [terms] are connected with *kṛts*.
(128) And it has no nature of sprouting again.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of that which is prohibited here, such as a magical creation (*nirmita*)," serves the purpose of connecting it with what was previously stated.
(129) The destruction of such a person wearing the sectarian mark is thus [brought about].
"Of such a kind" means one whose nature is not to sprout again; "the bearer of the mark" (liṅgin) refers to one who has gone forth, that is, one who is fully ordained (upasaṃpanna).
However, for one who has become a householder but is living among the monks, there is neither loss nor [acquisition] by virtue of the purpose of maintaining oneself.
Now, those related to the *kṛt* suffixes and others are pointed out: (130) *nirmitaḥ*.
One should ask one who has approached for the sake of going forth, "Are you not a phantom? and the ordainers [should also ask];
they should neither grant the going forth nor confer full ordination upon a phantom.
"There is no quality of sprouting for this;
there is only destruction for such a person who bears the marks [of a monk].
This same principle should be applied elsewhere as well, in the case of eunuchs and so forth.
(131) A paṇḍaka.
Its fivefold nature is as follows.
"Of this" refers to the word "pada."
What is the fivefold [classification]?
(132) [It is] that which causes the manifestation of birth, partiality, attachment, envy, and calamity.
A *paṇḍaka* by birth is one who,
from birth itself, is neither female nor male.
Regarding the term *pakṣapaṇḍaka*: one who is female during the [lunar] fortnight (*pakṣa*) and male during the [other] fortnight is a *pakṣapaṇḍaka*;
here, a "fortnight" (*pakṣa*) refers to half a month.
"One whose manifestation occurs through attachment" refers to one who manifests when approached by another; he is an "attached paṇḍaka."
One for whom the manifestation [of virility] occurs upon seeing another man approaching his wife out of jealousy is an *īrṣyā-paṇḍaka* (one who is impotent through jealousy).
"One who has become [so] through an accident" refers to an accidental paṇḍaka, whose male organ has been destroyed by castration or similar means.
(133) Here, when the final [element] partakes of the fault, there is destruction.
"Of the last one" refers to the *āpat-paṇḍaka* (one who becomes impotent due to calamity).
Immediately he incurs the fault of being a paṇḍaka;
therefore, he must be expelled,
and not otherwise— this is the meaning.
(134) One who lives in community through theft.

He states the definition of this [offense]: for one who knows that the procedure (*vidhi*) for full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) has not been performed, or that it has not taken root, while on the second day there is a communal experience of the ritual together with the Saṅgha, that constitutes the actual offense.

This refers to one who knows that the procedure for full ordination—consisting of the motion (*jñapti*) and so forth—has not been carried out, or even if it were carried out, that it has not taken root.
Although it was not performed by way of formal ordination (*upasaṃpad*) due to a defect such as being under twenty years of age,
yet because he experienced the second ritual together with the Saṃgha, his status is that of one who dwells in communion through theft (*steyasaṃvāsika*).

But was it not said: "O Upāli, when two or three formal acts of *poṣadha* have been experienced together with monks who are established in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*), by this much one is a 'one who dwells in communion through theft' (*steyasaṃvāsika*)"?
Now, why has the phrase "or three" not been formulated as a separate rule (*sūtra*)?
Since this statement is not intended as a restrictive rule, but rather as an illustration of the continuity [of the argument]:
that one who begins the sequence perishes.
Otherwise, this determination of "two" is understood to mean "three" in the case of inhalation.
And consequently, it follows that this is artificial and merely conventional, not established by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
And here there is also a textual passage concerning the subject matter of the narrative:
by which [definition of] subject matter one who lives in common through theft (steyasaṃvāsika) is not to be ordained nor to be fully admitted into the order.

"If it is thought that one should be ordained and receive full admission on account of that very same matter," he said: "One by whom two or three *poṣadhas* have been experienced should not be ordained nor should he receive full admission;
however, one by whom even a single *poṣadha* has been experienced should be ordained and should receive full admission."
For indeed, Arhatship is not attained otherwise, nor by means of experiencing only one part, but through the experience of both.
Furthermore, the reasoning is this: because one who first engages in this [practice] does so with apprehension, falsity does not become his innate nature at that stage;
however, by practicing continuously, he arrives at identification with it. Now, [one might object]: "But..."
In that context, the taking of the *poṣadha* was mentioned;
why then, here, is it said that there is the experience of the result of all actions without distinction?
It is said: because this duty is included within that which is to be done in reliance upon the Saṃgha.
That which is equal to the Poṣadha is that other ritual acts as well have the nature of depending upon the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the mention of the *poṣadha* is established as an illustration.
In a formal act (*karma*) where the inquiry regarding the full ordination (*upasaṃpad-āpatti*) has not been completed, there is also a scriptural authority [to this effect]:

if one participates in a formal act of the Saṃgha—whether it be the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*—by means of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapticaturtha-karman*) while one is not fully ordained, then that person experiences the status of being "exposed" (*uddiṣṭānubhūti*) as a twelfth individual;
by this much, it is said that one becomes a "one who dwells in communion through theft" (*steyasaṃvāsaka*).

To the extent that the announcement of one who has not yet been ordained regarding his intention to go forth and so forth— characterized by what is not to be done— is dependent upon the entire Saṃgha, it belongs to the category of *saṃgha-karman* (formal acts of the community).
Therefore, the term "karman" (formal act) should also be understood here.

If, despite having attained [the stages of] the delight in going forth, the state of a śrāmaṇera, birth [into the community], private instruction, purity, inclusion, probation, and so forth, as well as the various realizations, one is nonetheless established as a thief living in communion (steyasaṃvāsika).
(135) One who has departed for the sake of the non-Buddhist outsiders.

In order to make known its true nature: (136) For one who has undertaken this going-forth and holds that view, having cast aside this robe as his banner, at the rising of dawn therein, [he realizes] the reality.
Thus it has been said:
"This [is for] one who has undertaken the going-forth" means that his going-forth is by way of undertaking;
"in the view of those" refers to the view of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

"Abiding in this [view] and holding that view" means having cast aside the robes of a Sugata’s monk, thinking, "I shall discard these robes. "By that banner" means by the banner of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
In that context, "there" refers to the state of a non-Buddhist;
at the rising of the dawn, the reality is the state of having entered among the non-Buddhists.
(137) That which is not done [by oneself] is also [considered theft], like [theft committed by another].

Having cast off the appearance of a Tathāgata and, having donned the desired emblem of a non-Buddhist ascetic, one dwells until the rising of the dawn— this is the assumption of the Tathāgata’s emblem,
not the view of a non-Buddhist.
This is that which has not been done.
Furthermore, if one were to fall into the state of a non-Buddhist even when this [precept] has not been transgressed,
it would be just like the case of theft.
Since theft is also included therein, the meaning is that there are two types of experience;
thus, the state of living with a thief has been explained.
(138–145) A matricide.
A killer of his father.
One who kills an Arhat.
One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
One who, with a malicious mind, causes the Tathāgata’s blood to flow.
One who violates a bhikṣuṇī.
Has he fallen into any one of the four *pārājika* offenses or not?
One has not accepted the reversal of signs, nor has one made the vow for going forth and full ordination.

Thus, "the reversal of the cause" means that the reversal of whatever cause—such as quarrels or disputes—leads to the performance of desired actions like the *tarjanīya* (reprimand) and so forth, is the absence of those quarrels, disputes, and the like.
For the non-acceptance of what has been proposed is the absence of being a means of proof.
(146) Full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) is the formal motion (*jñapti*) for patience (*kṣānti*).

Those who lack patience are not fully ordained; because they lack the capacity for ordination, the function of another form of patience is not considered "patience" [in this context], but rather the function of patience itself.
"Venerable monks,
regarding the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*), whether one performs the formal act of ordination (*upasampaditikaraṇa*) or performs it as a non-ordination (*anupasampaditikaraṇa*).
(VinSū 24)
The formal admission (upasaṃpad) within the immediate vicinity has been explained.
Regarding the performance of the formal admission, it was stated in the Nidāna that "the motion (jñapti) is indeed the acceptance (kṣānti)."
(147) If one has not attained full ordination,
the assembly [of monks] is once again the formal resolution.

Thus, if it is argued that full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) is untenable because the conditions—such as the absence of causing strife—are reversed, the meaning is that the ritual act (*karman*) must nevertheless be performed once the assembly (*sāmagrī*) is complete again.
(148) If it is falsely stated that [the object] was not seen, there shall be penance.
If one speaks falsely, saying "I did not see this offense," when an offense has indeed been committed, there is an expiation for him.
For one who possesses such a principle, the absence of penance for false speech should not be prescribed.
Those with severed hands, those with severed feet, those with fingers like serpent-hoods,
those without lips, those with variegated limbs, the very aged, and the very young.
The lame, the one with a ruptured tendon, the one-eyed, the one with a withered arm, the hunchback, and the dwarf;
those with goiters, the mute, the deaf, the cripple who crawls on a board, and the one with elephantiasis.
Those men who are cut off by women, cut off by burdens, and cut off from the path; those who are like palm trees severed at the base or like kandalī plants cut down—such indeed are these persons.
—were rejected by the Great Seer.
"Renunciation for one who is pleasing to behold, and full ordination for one who is pure—this has been proclaimed by the Fully Awakened One, who knows all and whose name is Truth. Thus it is said.
"Those whose hands were severed" refers to those whose hands were cut off at the wrist.
Those whose feet have been cut off—meaning those for whom there is a severance down to the ankle—are called "pādacchinnāḥ."
Those whose fingers on their hands resemble the hoods of serpents are called "those with hood-like fingers. Those who lack the pair of lips are called "lipless."

Those whose bodies bear variegated marks are "variegated-limbed" (citrāṅga); they are called "variegated-limbed" because their hands and other limbs are painted. [The expressions] such as "as if flowing incessantly" and so forth [apply to them].
"Excessively old" refers to those aged one hundred years and so forth;
"excessively young" refers to one who is less than seven years of age and incapable of being made to fly like a crow.
"Lame" means those who move with a limp because of their feet.
*Kāṇḍarika* refers to one whose gait is utterly ruined by *gṛdhrasī* wind in the thighs and flanks.
One-eyed means having only one eye.
A *kuṇi* is one who, having only the bare mark of a hand at the wrist, is incapable of performing even the slightest action.
One who has a goitre (*galagaṇḍa*)—that is, a swelling on the neck (*grīvā-gaṇḍikā*)—is called *galagaṇḍa*.
Mūka means one who is incapable of speech.
"Pīṭhasarpi" (the floor-crawler) means that, having placed both hands for the sake of support, he crawls with his four limbs;
"phakka" is another synonym for this.
[This refers to one] who is emaciated by women.
One whose virility is impaired by excessive indulgence with women,
and whose body is unhappy and cut off by women.

Likewise, because they are unable to bear the burden and because they lack the capacity for traveling on the path, they are respectively termed "burden-cut" (*bhāracchinna*) and "path-cut" (*mārgacchinna*).
Tālamuktās are those who vomit because they are unable to consume food properly.

Some say thus: those who, because their knots have been destroyed by the process of cessation, act as if they were walking while obstructed from going; and those who, being young, are likewise incapacitated and limited by internal ailments such as consumption and the like, and are afflicted by powerful decrepitude.
They are like kandalī plants that have been cut down, incapable in all their activities;
the meaning is that there is no loss of youth for them.
Thus ends the section concerning that which is to be grasped.
And the Chapter on Going Forth is completed.
(v) Included among the miscellaneous [offenses] (149): A royal official who has not been authorized by the king and who resides nearby.
In this regard, one who has entered the state of renunciation should be asked, "Are you not a royal soldier?
Furthermore, the ordainers must not grant the going forth or the full ordination to a royal soldier who has not been authorized by the king and who resides nearby.
This should be taught to one who takes up the path of the stages of going forth.
Whether it be a king, a lord over his realm, or anyone else— such as a nobleman— who is connected to that station, he is here the instructor from nearby.
(150) A thief has been identified.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used for the purpose of excluding one who has not been authorized by the king and one whose teacher is not nearby.

When someone approaches for the sake of going forth, [the candidate] should be asked, "Are you a thief? and "Are you one who carries a banner? and the ordainers should likewise ask; they must not grant the going forth or the full ordination to a thief or one who carries a banner.
Thus, even by this much, there is likewise the existence of a prescription here.
One who is recognized as a thief is one whose banner is raised;
where there is no state of being recognized for someone, there is no state of having one's banner raised for them.
(151) One should not ordain chariot-makers, leather-workers, caṇḍālas, pukkulas, or those of similar status.

The chariot-maker and the leather-worker—by the phrase "those of such a kind," it is indicated that chariot-makers and others are unfit for the stages of being a non-celibate novice (*abhokṣya-śrāmaṇera*), a trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), or full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*); this unfitness is the reason for their exclusion from going forth (*apravrājana*).
Therefore, this establishes that they also are not to perform these [acts].
(152) The illustration consists of those whose hands have been severed, and so forth.

That which has been stated in the section on going forth (*pravrajyāvastu*) as an illustration— beginning with "those whose hands are severed" and "those whose feet are severed"— should be understood as an illustration (*nidarśana*),
not as an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*).
He now introduces those for whom this serves as an illustration:
Those with turmeric-colored hair, golden hair, and likewise green hair; those with pure white hair, men with serpent-like hair, and those who are hairless;
those with severed heads, those with many heads, those who are excessively corpulent, and those who are emaciated.
And those with heads like donkeys or pigs, those with two heads, or those with tiny heads;
those with ears like elephants, horses, oxen, or monkeys.
Some have ears like those of donkeys or pigs, some have but a single ear, and some have no ears at all;
some have red eyes, some have excessively large eyes, some have sunken eyes, and some are deep tawny;
some have eyes like glass, some have eyes like bubbles, some have but a single eye, and some have no eyes at all.
Those with noses like elephants, horses, oxen, and monkeys; those with noses like donkeys and pigs; those with a single nose, and those who are noseless;
those with jaws like elephants, horses, oxen, and monkeys.
Those with teeth like donkeys or pigs, those with a single tooth, and those without teeth; those with teeth like elephants, horses, oxen, or monkeys;
those with teeth like donkeys or pigs, those with a single tooth, and those without teeth.
Those with protruding necks and those without necks, those with drooping shoulders and those who are excessively hunchbacked;
those with severed tails, those with testicles like wind-bags, those with only one testicle, and even those without testicles;
those who are too tall and those who are too short, those who are emaciated and those who suffer from excessive leprosy.
And with four types of skin colors, as well as those who are leprous or deformed;
even toward such persons, one should maintain that same respectful conduct.
The meaning is that one should maintain such an attitude even toward those who reject [the teaching] by saying "him" or "those with severed hands," "those with severed feet," and so forth.
Those whose hair is red like turmeric are *haridrakeśāḥ*;
those with lion-like hair are *siṃhakeśāḥ*; those with golden hair are *harikeśāḥ*.
Those whose hair is dyed like indigo are "green-haired" (haritakeśaḥ).
Those whose hair is naturally white from birth are called *avadātakeśāḥ*, meaning they have pure white hair, but are not grey-haired.
Those whose hair is like that of an elephant are called *nāgakeśa*.
Those whose heads are smooth like a copper vessel and devoid of hair are called *akeśaka*.
He who has three or four thick ridges on his head,
by which depressions and elevations are discernible,
is a *ghāṭośiras*.
Those whose bodies are as if swollen with fat are possessed of bulkiness.
Those ripenings of yours are distinct and contracted.
He whose eyes are excessively small and round has crushed eyes (or sunken eyes).
Because his eyes have entered inside his head, he is one whose eyes are situated in his shoulders; thus, he is Skandhākṣa.
He whose tail is the organ of excretion, and that [tail] of his has been cut off, is one whose tail is severed (lāṅgūlachinna).
Those for whom even a slight activity gives rise to extraordinary exhaustion are "excessively weary" (atikilāsinaḥ); this is a designation for exhaustion (klama).
And by the four complexions—namely, blue, yellow, red, and white—they are of censurable form;
it is only such specific types of complexion that are rejected, but not those of praiseworthy form like that of the gods.
Thus, for the time being, the ordination and so forth of such persons have been rejected;
he speaks next in order to demonstrate that there is also no inclusion of those who have already gone forth and received full ordination [if they are of such a nature].
(153) One should not provide support for a renunciant who is corrupted by birth or body.
One should not ordain those such as chariot-makers who are unfit for food because they are corrupted by birth;
nor those such as those with severed hands, who are corrupted by their complexion or physical form through the body.
(VinSū 27) One should not ordain them.
It also occurs when providing a dwelling place or giving internal gifts, not merely by way of providing formal reliance (*niśraya*).
And likewise, a monk must not ordain a corrupt assembly;
if he ordains one, he commits an offense of transgression.
Having said this, by how much may an assembly be called a "corrupt assembly"?
By way of birth, as well as by color and physical form.
How is it by birth?
From the families of chariot-makers, caṇḍālas, and pukkasas.
How [are they distinguished] by color and shape?
It is stated here: "those with turmeric-colored hair," and so forth.
(154) It is not permissible for a single preceptor to confer full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) upon a single person with a single utterance;
rather, it is [permissible] for many, meaning two or more.
"A single preceptor" means one who has a single preceptor; [the term refers to] such a person.
"By a single word" means by a single designation (*prajñapti*). From what [does this follow]? He says: "Because of multiplicity," that is, because it is applicable up to three.
The meaning is "not by another," based on the traditional teaching (āgama) that "one group does not perform the actions of another group."

Some, having accepted a distinction between the teachers, compose a text here: "Venerable sir, is it possible that at one time, in one moment, by a single agent of action, through a single act of informing, two actions have been performed and must be declared,
yet the Saṃgha does not become exhausted by that?"

"It is possible, Upāli, if that monk who performs the ritual is capable of proclaiming the names of the preceptors and does not omit the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the performance of the ritual for those seeking full ordination," and so forth.
The two novices, Pālaka and Dāsaka, who were the attendants of the noble Upāli, went along with affection;
because they were mutually protective of one another, they should not be ordained simultaneously.
Therefore, two are not ordained separately [at the same time].
On account of this cause, the permission for one preceptor to ordain many [disciples] was granted; from this cause, the acceptance of many by one preceptor is seen here due to this very cause.
Thus it has been accepted, yet it is not put into practice.
(155) There is an absence of mutual agreement among those who hold the same views.

For those who have received full ordination at the same time through a single formal act of motion (*karmavācanā*), or even for those who were ordained separately but at an identical time, there is no mutual obligation of performing services of respect toward one another.
Reverential salutation is the act of homage.
(156) When [the state of being] attained, it is the first.

For those who have equal seniority, the basis for determining the distribution of gains, the assignment of duties, and so forth, is the principle that whoever arrives first has the priority in receiving the gains, according to the statement: "Gains should be accepted according to the order of arrival."

One who arrives later at the commencement of the ritual must perform the preliminary rites first, because of the statement: "The one who arrives later [performs] the first [rites] at the commencement. The meaning is this: when the first position is reached upon receiving the offerings, that constitutes priority.
Regarding the performance of the undertaking of action, when the five stages have been reached, there is primacy [of the first].
(157) A forest-dweller shall not let his hair grow longer than two finger-breadths.
(158) This is not so, because of its proximity; [therefore] he is a village-dweller.
The state of being proximal is "proximity" (arvāktvam).
Because of this proximity within two finger-breadths, the measure of one and a half finger-breadths is attained above that;
it should be understood that knowledge arises [in the practitioner] regarding the point at which [the breath] should no longer be retained.
The text here is as follows: "A forest-dwelling monk (āraṇyaka) must maintain a hair-tuft (bālā) two finger-breadths in length;
one who dwells near a village (grāmāntika) may keep it shorter than that."
Some read "dvyaṅgulāvartā" in place of "dvyaṅgula";
if the meaning of this reading is "those whose coils (āvarta) measure two fingers (dvyaṅgula)," there is no difference in substance from the previous reading.
Now, the claim that "two finger-breadths" refers to a curl is incorrect;
because it has become the state of the disappearance of the *liṅga*, its length is of this [specified] measure. (VinSū 28)
For the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was prescribed by him on account of that specific causal fault, and since that very state of falling into such a fault still persists;
because the measure [of hair] is more than five finger-breadths,
it is logical that shaving and so forth should be performed even after the time of ordination (*pravrajyā*), following the procedure for shaving and so forth at the time of going forth.
Thus, its insertion occurs in this place.
(159–162) He shall not have his hair cut in the shape of a cow’s tail.
Excluding the vicinity of the wound.
One should not have the topknot cut.
One should not have hair removed from a congested area.
Thus it is said.
The phrase "one should not cause [it] to be done" is to be supplied as a continuation.
A "constricted place" refers to the private parts.
(163) One should have [the robe] made for the purpose of covering a wound while it is still unhealed; otherwise, one must consult the elder and senior monks who are wise.
"If they have not ascended, it is otherwise. The Blessed One said: "It must first be purified by the five astringents (*kaṣāya*);
afterwards, if health is still not restored,"

The text states: "Having consulted with the monks who are holders of the Sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkās, one should have the facial hair trimmed when it has become overgrown.
In this regard, this is the illustration:
while the prescribed method for lamentation is appropriate, other modes of medical treatment are also included therein.
"Having observed the elder monks, one should have hair removal performed in a crowded area for the purpose of [checking] a wound or for the purpose of [detecting] a living creature.
Regarding this, there is another textual tradition which states that "observing" refers to what was done in the presence of those who are well-known.
And by two types of elders— superiority in terms of moral discipline and through mastery of the Dharma and Vinaya—
both of these are included therein as being observed and understood;
the statement regarding "being a bearer of the Piṭakas" refers to such understanding.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of living beings," the intention here refers to living beings located within a wound,
not to lice and the like;
and since this [wound] is already included by virtue of being the cause of the wound itself, it is not mentioned separately.
(164) One should not even cause a woman's vein to be used for that purpose.
"Atannimittam" means the sign of being free from wounds;
"jaṅghāmuṇḍanam" refers to the channel of the limbs.
(165) Not elsewhere than in the body.
Thus it is said.
This prohibition regarding the grooming of body hair applies to that bodily conduct other than the two channels of the private parts, starting from the neck upwards;

therefore, by this [rule], there is no prohibition against the necessity of attending to the hair of the head and beard. As for the hair of the nose, it is well known that there was no statement regarding its removal; such is the established understanding.
In this regard, the text in the *Mātṛkā* states: "Having left the hair of the head and beard as they are, one must not have the hair removed from any other parts of the body or limbs.
Whoever should have it removed commits a *duṣkṛta*; it is an offense."
(166–168) One may use a razor-edged instrument, a nail-cutter, or an axe-head;
however, one should not polish these.
One should apply ointment for the removal of dirt;
however, one should not shave the hair of the head or the beard with a garment.
In this context, it is appropriate to understand "upper garment" (*upariprāvaraṇa*) as referring to the outer cloak (*saṃghāṭī*),
and not to the inner robe (*antarvāsas*); nor does it apply to every upper garment, but specifically to the outer cloak and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
In this case, another upper garment is appropriate for that which has already been worn;
for here, the ground for rejection is established.
(169) One should wear a hair-net.
Thus, "cīvara" refers to the hair-receptacle;
its utility is precisely for that purpose. As for the etymology: it is that by which hair is received.
How is it known that this is called "robe" (*cīvara*)?
It is because of the statement in the consecration mantra: "The robe is the receptacle for receiving the hair; it is the basis.
Furthermore, how is it understood that its purpose is for wearing?
It is not, however, for the purpose of shaving the hair right there;
for the *saṃkakṣikā* is mentioned in the context of its absence.
Indeed, the shaving of hair is not prohibited when one is wearing a *saṃkakṣikā*.
(170) In its absence, [it may be covered] with a *saṃkakṣikā*.
In the absence of a robe for receiving hair, one should have the hair and beard shaved while the *saṃkakṣikā* is worn to cover [the body].
(171) "Not on a rug"—
thus one should not have one's hair and beard shaved.
Even in the *Nidānas*, this section of the text concludes with the statement that nail-clipping must be done at the very beginning.
(172) One should not place the communal broom there.
Thus, this pertains to the authority over the monasteries.
One should cause [the image] to be brought down from a temple or similar structure if it is decayed, if one is ill, or during wind, heat, or rain.
One should prepare that place.
The preparation consists of removing all hair and ensuring it is free of water;
it should be done in such a way that these conditions are fulfilled.
(175) When [the ground] is strewn [with grass], one should utter the words "bāla."
The meaning is: in a place containing residual formations (saṃskāra).
(176) Thus [is the rule for] clipping the nails.
The phrase beginning with "not on a spread" (*na saṃstare*) is an extended application (*atideśa*).
When [the hair] is being carefully grasped during the reception of the hair, it is considered as having been placed on the ground;
therefore, there is no cutting here where the communal broom (*saṃdhika-saṃmārjanī*) falls.
Thus, one should understand that this [act] is either something already transcended or that the stage [of practice] has become incapable of further preparation;
therefore, the possibility of this exemption for the removal of hair and beard must be recognized as non-existent.
(177) A nun who has not been authorized by a man free from passion must not cut her hair.
"This [nun]" refers to one who is not free from passion; "there is no offense if she were free from passion"—this is the text in that regard.
"She should cut them" is a statement concerning the shaving of the head.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred Śākyāyanī nuns, herself cut off her hair.
"Having donned saffron-colored robes"— this refers to the cutting of hair, because she was designated as "shaven-headed" by the statement, "[In this very way, Gautamī,
you shall be beautiful though shaven-headed]"; since her hair was long, this designation was made for a specific reason regarding her being shorn of it.
Except for conventional usage—the meaning is that a nun who has not yet abandoned passion, if she is not authorized by another nun, shall not have her hair cut by a man.

(178) To her who is becoming impassioned, the presiding authority should instruct: "Establish mindfulness; what essence is there in this body? The phrase "to her who is becoming impassioned" refers to that nun who is performing the ritual preparation (*kalpaka*).

(179) "One should establish the perception of her as a mother, a sister, or a daughter," it is said in the *Kalpaka*. To one who is becoming lustful, the presiding nun should instruct: "Establish the perception of her as a mother and so forth."
(180) Having performed [the preliminary rites] here, one should perform the ritual bath.
"Here" refers to the shaving of the hair and beard.
(181) Or, purity consists of five factors.
Or the word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of including another alternative interpretation.
Even though water is available, this is indeed permissible: "A bhikṣu may keep hair-clippers,
or he may bathe."
The text continues: "Finally, one's hands and feet should be washed. Thus ends the passage.
(182) "One should not bathe naked":
when the three circles [of the body] are covered, there is complete non-nakedness;
as long as the three circles are covered, the hair on the limbs and the body is likewise covered.
In this context, it must be understood by implication that because everything [else] is concealed, there is nothing further to be avoided.
(183) A bhikṣuṇī shall not bathe at a bathing place for men, nor with powder at a bathing place for women.
At a *puruṣatīrtha*, bathing for a female mendicant is strictly prohibited; however,
at a *strītīrtha*, she may perform a partial bath (*kevala*) using substances such as mung bean flour.
There was a lack of understanding:
"The group of twelve nuns were bathing at a ford used by women;
they were acting with levity toward the wives of householders who were bathing there."
They throw māṣa flour and other substances [into the water].
The Blessed One said: "A bhikṣuṇī must not bathe with powder at a bathing place for women. This is the text on this point.
(184) It is conceived [as follows]: the powder of mung beans and so forth is permeated with fragrance. (VinSū 30)
Universal eligibility applies here.
(185–186) Its acceptance [is as follows].
And by one who is ill, [it should be used] after having been infused with medicine.
Thus, the word "imagines" (kalpayate) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis.
(187) A bhikṣuṇī shall not throw powder at a woman.

Because no specific distinction is made— such as "at the time of bathing" or "at other times"— the practice [of wearing clothes] is stated here in order to avoid the undesirable consequence of [the practitioner] being naked.
(188) One should not ascend a ladder with the ends of one's lower garment tucked up and not fastened behind or in front.
The meaning is: by that which has the front, back, and lower parts of the garment fastened together at the bottom;
this is for the purpose of avoiding the exposure of the private parts (*kaupīna*).
Furthermore, even when climbing trees and the like, there is the awareness of the sight of one's private parts.
Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of "climbing" here is merely illustrative.
When one climbs in times of distress for the sake of a remedy, if the climbing is obstructed by the very sewing of his garment, he must preserve it;
if it is not so obstructed, he may go because climbing trees is permitted.
(189) It could not be otherwise at another time.

The meaning is that at other times, having ascended the ladder, one should not have the lower garment tied, nor should one wear it with the front and back parts reversed; rather, one should remain in a state of proper decorum (*sāmīcī*).
Regarding the phrase "the private parts being on the side," this refers to the avoidance of nakedness in this particular place.
One should not resort to a covering for one whose face is uncovered.
One should not resort to that covering which is an uncovered state for one whose face is not covered by clothing and the like;
"a monk yawning should cover his mouth with his hand"—this is the scriptural text here.
In this context, the hand is established as the means of covering.
And regarding yawning and acting according to one's desire, this was said with reference to what is well known as their suppression;
when there is no capacity [to suppress them], there is no fault in not practicing that [suppression].
One should wear a bathing garment.
Attachment (*āsakti*) refers to the state of living beings within the two-fold [world].
It should be called "clinging" (*sakti*); the prefix *ā-* is employed for the sake of indicating completion (*saṃpatti*), as this is a designation of the cause.
Since there is an attachment of living beings to a double-layered garment,
the meaning is that one should not bathe in water containing living beings while wearing such a garment.
(193) "One who possesses only the three robes" means:
"One should wear a bathing cloth"—this is the connection.
The text here states: "The Blessed One said: 'A monk who possesses only three robes must wear a bathing cloth.'"
Some maintain that "it should be kept without being formally resolved upon" (*anadhiṣṭhāya dhārayitavyaḥ*); however, this is incorrect.
Since the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) arises when one has obtained a bathing-garment without having formed the formal intention (*saṃkalpa*), this intention must necessarily be generated in this case.
And once it is generated, the necessity of performing a mental resolve (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in this regard is established.

Therefore, it is logical that the undertaking of another basis is possible because it is easy to perform; and from this very permission, it should be understood that there is no breach of his undertaking by means of this [physical act].
(194) Having placed leaves in front and behind, one should bathe in a secluded place.
Not all [monks] were indeed restricted to the three robes alone.
[In this regard, there is a textual passage: For others, there was no acquisition of a bathing cloth;
the Blessed One said, "They should bathe in a secluded place after placing leaves in front and behind [themselves]. This was stated without distinction [between those with and without such a cloth].
(195) By means of liberation, there is the removal of the fettered living being from the lower realms.
Because there is excessive attachment to a single layer [of cloth], whereas for living beings there is [safety] in a double layer, this is the established practice.
It is not that the state of being double-layered is absent from his garment;
therefore, it should be understood that the settled rule is: "One must not bathe in water containing living beings with this [garment]."
(196) This [rule] applies in a monastery where there is a mirage of water. (VinSū 31)
Regarding the phrase "if in the monastery": this bathing should be performed only within the water-vessel (udakabhrama) and not elsewhere.
(197) And the discarding of a liquid substance.
Thus, the discarding of liquid substances such as those used for washing the feet is only when there is the delusion that they are water, and not otherwise.
(198–199) The construction of a bathhouse.
In this [context], there is the taking up of the layer of bricks.
In this bathing hall.
(200) The release from the delusion of water; the purification of the stream.
The Blessed One said: "It should be called a water-hallucination."
There was a drainage channel;
the Blessed One said,
"It should be cleaned from time to time."
Rather, one must bathe in the very mirage of water; for the purpose of including that, he says:
(201) When one has bathed in delusion, there is no rising up.
The term "syandanikāyāḥ" is a continuation [of the previous context].
"Snātiḥ" means bathing. This is an explanation of the technical term "syandanikā."
When bathing occurs by mistake, there should be no cleaning of the drain;
however, it is not a restrictive rule that one must bathe only when in error,
because the purpose of the gutter is for bathing.
(202) One should cleanse the body with rubbing and scrubbing, but not the feet.
The text states: "A monk must not rub his body with a brush.
The word "another" refers to something other than the foot;
however, there is no prohibition regarding those two [the hands and feet].

(203) This is an illustration of the "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) and the "courageous" (*śauṭīra*). To the question of what kind of substance performs such an act, he says: "sharp weapons and the like," and "the courageous," such as Śaunaka and others, because they bring about a transformation of the mind.
The Blessed One commanded: "The body must not be rubbed with a conch shell.
The monks rubbed it with a [plain] conch shell, so the Blessed One said: "A hollowed-out conch shell (muṇḍa-śukti) should be made"; this is the textual passage on the matter.
For here, because of its sharpness, sour gruel (śukti) is prohibited;
therefore, it serves as an illustration.
One should not rub the body with any other substance that is likewise sharp or harsh.
(204) Purification of conch-shell by means of fire.
And its purification by fire consists merely in heating it;
otherwise, the whiteness would be destroyed.
(205) A nun who has committed the offense of *āmuṣṭicailavarta* shall not rub herself with anything by anyone.
The body is nothing at all;
it is the body of a young woman, yet even more than something soft and smooth, it is subject to transformation.
Even if it is very close [to the body], for women to perform this act constitutes an act of boldness; thus, there is a total prohibition regarding nuns.
"A little" means a garment that is somewhat delicate or soft.
Having stated that it is merely the size of a fist, [he] quotes the words of Cailavarti.
(206) One should not put on the robes without having removed the water used for washing.

This is for the purpose of avoiding the loss of a robe that is being worn; therefore, the understanding is that it belongs to whichever person the water has not yet left. This applies to one who does not wish to wait for the formal ritual of dedication (*ādhāna*).
With respect to that, the two subsequent rules are prescribed.
One should keep a cloth for wiping the body.
In the absence [of water], having remained for a moment in the *utkuṭuka* posture, one should wipe oneself with a bathing cloth.

Or, to the extent that this [robe] is complete for the purpose of bathing, wearing, and wiping, to whatever measure of time it remains so complete—that is what is indicated here by the term "muhūrta. Or, it is a designation for any small duration of time;
having stood in the squatting posture (utkuṭuka), in this way there is the rapid removal of water from the body, and this position is one of concealed form.
Therefore, it is not appropriate for this one who is without a protector to resort to [another]; this is the point of taking refuge.
(209–210) One should resort to a steam bath.
The construction of a basket is best performed on ground free of gravel.
A *karaṇḍaka* is a dwelling for the purpose of a latrine;
a *karaṇḍa* should be constructed in a place that is elevated and strewn with gravel (*uccharkara*). (VinSū 32)
Regarding this, the text states: "Even when [a word] has gone to another region, it is [still considered] *sampadyate* (correctly formed) because its meaning is not incomplete;

however, in the case of *uccharkara*, there is correctness (*sādhutva*) because it accomplishes the complete sense. This is the meaning. It should be understood that the same applies here to the employment of the word "correct" (*sādhu*).
To show what should be done regarding that casket, he says:
(211) "In the center, there is an opening for a window that is circular on the outside, spacious within, and shaped like the ocean."
The meaning is that it is neither below nor above, but within the middle of the wall inside the casket.
(212) Herein is the installation of the latticed window, the door-bolt, the wheel, the small jar, and the needle.
"Here" means at the window.
(213) And the infliction of the staff upon one who has committed an offense against an innocent person.
The word "and" (ca) is intended to introduce the connection of the term "here" (atra).
With that staff having a goat-foot [at its end], a needle is inserted into the window and withdrawn.
(214) At the door, one should apply a bolt, a crossbar, and a ring to the frame of the door-panel.
"Door" refers to the opening of the casket.
(215) The construction of an inner side parapet wall for the purpose of holding heated water.
The *piṇḍikā* here is the cornice (*kapoṭamālā*) upon which water-jars are placed.
(216–217) At the site for the fire-ritual, one should place a layer of bricks upon the ground.
The ritual for the extinction of the fire.
Thus is the rounding off.
(218) For that purpose, there is the wearing of an iron buttock-patch.
"For that purpose" means for the purpose of the destruction by fire.
(219) When fire is blazing, one should avoid entering it without weariness.
In the sauna hall.
(220) To prevent the arising of darkness, one should cast into the fire barley-meal that has been smeared with pungent oil.
Agnimadā is tamikā.
(221) Incense is offered for the sake of removing foul odors.
That foul odor which was produced by those groats.
(222–223) The remedy for holding quick-drying oil using a ball of *cikkasa* powder.
And with a cluster of *āmalaka* fruits;
here, "a cluster under the arm" refers to the seat.
In this regard, regarding the seat with a bolster in the steam-bath (jentāka),
it is not for the purpose of sitting upon it after being anointed with oil;
thus its permission is granted.
(224) The spreading of grass upon the ground refers to moist grass, or to fresh, naturally occurring, or soaked [grass].
In that context, "inherent" (autpattika) refers to that moisture which exists by its very nature; [in the absence of that], one must rely on the moisture produced by moistening.
Here, the meaning is "non-burning."
(225–226–227–228) The making of an iron scraper for the purpose of scratching.
Having tied it with a thread made of *cidra* grass, its placement is to be done by the *upadhivārika* in a secret location.
For the sake of perfecting its polish, the application of fire is performed upon it.
There, one should not bathe.
In that regard, "there" means in the womb.
(229) The construction of a hall for that purpose.
"For that purpose" means for the purpose of bathing.
(230) To prevent the robes from being soaked [by rain], one should construct a pit lined with bricks.
In order to avoid the destruction of robes being washed, one who has descended into a pit should bathe, while one standing on high ground should offer water;
by this, it should be understood that a transgression has occurred.
(231) This liberation from the delusion of water.
"Of this" refers to the pit.
(232) "Announcing hot water to those remaining" means that, having ascertained that the water is warm, one should inform the other renunciants.
(233) Its dissolution occurs through cold.
Of hot water.
(234) Also at the beginning of the consecration and so forth.
Even for the purpose of sprinkling and so forth, there is a distinction between this [fire] and cold [water].
(235–239) The presentation of a bowl filled with pebbles, cow dung, and tooth-sticks.
If there is a state of weakness, it is for the purpose of creating prior devotion;
if one attends by remaining neutral,
being unknown [to the matter], then one should ask him who has arrived here for the sake of full knowledge.
[The gatekeeper was stationed for this purpose.]
And for the purpose of preventing the entry of a monk.
"By way of inclusion" means by including oneself as one of you;
"gone there" means gone to the *jentāka* (steam-bath house).
One should ask in order to ascertain: "Is this a monk, or is he an Ājīvika, or the like?"

The purpose of appointing a gatekeeper for this reason is for the sake of interrogation and for the sake of preventing entry, in order to ascertain whether one who approaches by falling among those unknown [to the community] is actually known or not.
By means of the question, "Are you one of us?", he is identified.
To what kind of person does the gatekeeper belong? He says: to a monk (bhikṣu).
This is an illustration [applying] even to one who has gone forth but is not fully ordained;
or it applies to nuns, or to a person belonging to their faction.
(240) One should not grant entry here to one who lacks faith.

"In this place" means in the steam-bath (*jentāka*). Even for one who is attending [to others], it is by way of being included in the middle; this is another meaning of "gatekeeper" (*dvārapāla*) in this context.
(241) Here, the preparation is to be performed by the co-residents and the resident pupils.
"Here" means in the steam-bath house.
(242) "It is new" means it is another.
This is a presentation of another opinion; it is a variant reading held by some that the preliminary purification (parikarma) should be performed in the Jantāka with nine [verses].
Regarding the preparatory cultivation for the purpose of seeing forms, he says:
(243–244) The performance of services for one another—such as providing lamps, basins, oil, tooth-sticks, cow dung, powdered earth, water, and so forth; the inspection of wooden items;

and the acts of anointing with unguents, bathing, sweeping, clearing away refuse, and other such duties—this is the mutual performance of services, such as anointing and the like, between co-residents and disciples.
Having cleansed both the seat and the oyster-shell, they should be placed in their proper positions.
By such words as these,
the summary of the preparatory rites (*parikarma*) required [for the practice] is presented in the *Mātṛkā*, from the beginning up to the end of the passage ending with "he should fan" (*vitapet*).
(246) This rule applies to every vessel.
Having ensured cleanliness, placing it in its proper place—this is "this."
(247) One should ensure that all equipment is well-concealed and carried away.
There is no non-taking of any utensil by means of taking "belongings" (*bhāṇḍa*), except for the garments of a monk. This sūtra is for the purpose of providing a formal rule (*vidhāna*).
(248) One should enter here with little noise.
In the bathhouse.
(249–250) He is pleasing;
he is well-restrained and possesses a pleasing deportment through clear comprehension.
Being well-restrained in his own conduct, he demonstrates non-distraction through the state of being well-restrained in body and speech.
By the phrase "being clearly conscious," the clarity of the mind regarding the postures is shown through these two modes.
(251) One should not fan [the fire] while standing in front of it.
The meaning is that one should not cause oneself to suffer by placing a barrier between oneself and another who is suffering.
This refers to "avoiding social distraction."
The phrase "here" carries over from the previous context;
having entered the *jentāka* (steam bath) in accordance with one's desires,
since it has been said that "socializing is an inflamer of desires," its avoidance here is particularly emphasized.
(253) It is the reliance upon the noble silence.
The word "here" is indeed connected [to this].
This sūtra is for the purpose of turning away the mind from non-existent conceptual constructions and their corresponding tendencies.
It should be understood that the noble silence consists in the manifestation of thorough mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
(254) Taking up the triple staff when one is about to depart.
At the time of going.
(255) One who has not mastered even a single verse should not perform the preparatory rite.
In this context, some take the term *jentāka* to mean the mutual assistance rendered to one another as manifested within the body;
that is, monks wearing only a single robe (*ekacīvara*) should not perform services for one another in a sauna (*jentāka*).
This applies to all forms of service, not only those involving the body, and at all locations. (VinSū 34)
Since this rule does not apply exclusively to the steam-bath house (jentāka),
it is not dependent upon that.
(256) One should not cause this to be done by a body lacking faith.
"Etad" refers to the preparatory practice (parikarma), which is that external activity such as carrying burdens and so forth that is not prohibited.
(257) Here and in the preceding [verse], non-remissness and faith are intended.
‘Non-fluctuating’ (*anitvarā*) means that which is unshakable due to its arising after a long period of time.
‘In this’ (*atra*) refers to the previously mentioned method of purification (*parikarmavidhi*).
‘And in the preceding [passage]’ (*pūrvatra ca*) refers to the statement: “One should not grant entry here to one who lacks faith.”
"Abhisaṃhitā" means intended.
(258) One who is like a lion should not behave like a jackal.
The meaning is that one who possesses ethical discipline should not provide service to one who lacks it;
rather, reproach is directed toward the latter.
(259–260) One should attend upon preceptors and instructors who are of extremely immoral conduct.
And also toward one's mother, father, and the sick, even those who are householders.
This permission is granted because they are of the greatest benefit.
(261) Bathing is performed with the bathing of the ritual requisites.
[The sick person:
Regarding this, the following introductory account is recited:
"In the formal rule (prajñapti), the mention of 'the sick' was not made."

Nor is there a lack of correspondence in anything else, because it is not grasped as a specific distinction; rather, it is formulated as pertaining to all bases. To demonstrate its own nature, he says:
(262) A bath with a decoction of the roots, tubers, leaves, flowers, and fruits of plants that remove wind is called by that same name.
The meaning is that it is called the "bath of the equipment" (saṃbhāraka-snātra).
The purpose [of these] in the bath is nourishment;
thus, these constitute the ancillary elements (aṅga) here.
He explains how the bath is performed: //
(263–264) Anointing with unguents is for the sake of smoothness;
bathing with perfumed water is for the removal of that [stain].
For the purpose of removing that unctuous substance, such as oil and so forth, there is the *upasnānaka*— that is to say, the application of cleansing agents (*abhyakṣā*).
(265) [For the previous purpose: one should place two or three drops of oil into the water jar in the west.
"For the sake of the previous purpose" means for the sake of smoothness.
The meaning is that two or three drops of oil should be poured into the final water-jar.
(266) One should bathe in an iron tub;
one who is ill should keep this [tub].
"Enām" refers to this iron bowl.
It is not proper for one who is not ill to carry it,
nor to use it, as it is like a lump of iron.
This is how it should be understood:
the performance of such a kind of frivolity for a purpose other than that [intended]—
and since all of that is understood to be a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), it has not been explicitly formulated as a rule in the Sūtra.
One should place a lid over it.
For the purpose of avoiding the state of coldness in hot water.
And here, upon the neck, [he places] a pillow for the cheek.
The word "should give" carries over [from the previous rule].
Here, the bathing should be performed without delay,
for the sake of avoiding suffering.
Therefore, there is the giving of this [perfection].
(269) One should not wash one's feet anywhere at all.
This concerns the superintendent of the monastery.
(270) Its location is the opening of the *pranāḍī*.
"Of this" refers to the washing of the feet.
Regarding the Blessed One's statement, "It should be washed at the mouth of the drain," such is the text.
(271) They should have a foot-washing basin made;
for without this, there would be an obstruction to the accomplishment of the purpose at the mouth of the conduit and so forth.
Thus, in this matter, there is freedom of choice.
The use of the verb at the beginning is for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no fixed rule;
its locus is communal property (*sāṃghika-vastu*). And since the application of this [offense] does not occur to a single person regarding communal property, the plural form is used.
He states in which location: //
In the southeast corner of the upper chamber.
"What is its form?"— (273) it has the shape of a pestle; here, the meaning is the removal of impurities.
(274) One should set out a stone slab for washing.
This is the name for receiving [a gift].
To the question "Of what material is it? he says: "It is made of clay."
One should not set out washing-slabs made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal;
rather, they should be made of clay—this is the text here. As for their shape:

(275) "With a base like an elephant's foot and possessing a pericarp (*karṇikā*). Here, the meaning is "not rolling about. The phrase "possessing a pericarp" refers to this being made for the purpose of supporting the feet while they are being washed.
He says that it possesses [the lotus] by means of which pericarp it is situated: //
(276) Regarding the one situated in the center, he asks: "Of what form is she? and replies:—
(277) And it is rough, having the shape of a kadamba flower.
The feet are rough for the purpose of preventing slipping.
(278) Having washed [the vessel], the placement of it with its opening facing downwards.
This washing is for the sake of being pleasing;
"purity" means being pleasing.
And there is no water for cleansing that remains therein.
Therefore, there is no attainment [of the goal] from that; thus, it should be understood that [the washing must be done] with other water.
This is the meaning of the text: "Having washed his feet outside the vihāra, or having discarded the foot-washing water at the mouth of a drain, he should wash them again."
He states where the placement is: //
(279–282) On top of the terrace, [the rule applies] to the communal [lodging];
in a private cell, it applies to the pair of door-leaves.
In whatever area of the monastery one performs tasks such as washing the alms-bowl, that place should be swept or smeared with water.
"In the shape of a spearhead or a drum"—
the word "shape" (ākāreṇa) continues [from the previous context].
To the question "With what is the plastering done?", he says:
(283) With cow dung or with clay.
[Thus it is said].
(284) In the case of the pursuit of jewels, there is no fixed rule regarding the appearance of what is smeared.
(285–287) They should not cause one who is unworthy to go forth, nor should they confer full ordination upon such a person.
Or by the additional [measure] of nine *pāṇḍus*:
there are three bowls,
namely the large, the medium, and the small.
To determine its measure, it is said: (288) From the remainder, starting from the interior of the thumb up to the top of the vessel, or above a *prastha* of cooked rice;
or, from that [measure], two *māgadha* measures of food together with soup and condiments—this is the medium [portion]. This is what should be known.
It is not of the upper part nor of the lower part;
finally, it is not from any other region immediately following, but rather that which is the interior of the thumb.
The width of the thumb at its knuckle is the measure;
by that remaining lower portion, it is a Magadhan *prastha* of cooked rice,
or else double that amount, a *prastha*.
As long as one carries [the substance] together with its appropriate condiments until it is fully cooked, that is "unimpaired" (*anapeta*), meaning it has attained its proper state (*āpya*).
A Magadhan *prastha* consists of thirty-two *palas* of oil, ghee, honey, water, and so forth.
Of the other non-fluid substances, there are sixteen; these are the manifestors of mere substance.
Therefore, it should be understood that sixteen palas here are designated by means of the Māgadha-prastha measure.

“That in which two Magadhan prasthas of cooked rice, along with soup and condiments, are placed such that they do not touch the sides of the thumb’s hollow—that is the superior [vessel]. That in which there is one [prastha] is the inferior; between these two is the middling.”
In this passage,

because the soup (*sūpa*) and the condiments (*vyañjana*) are included here as things to be seasoned (*vyañjanīya*), it is understood that the soup and condiments possess the quality of being a *temana* (seasoning) in their respective portions;
therefore, since there is a plurality of distinct condiments, they are to be applied here in their individual parts.

In order to eliminate the defects of deficiency, mediocrity, excellence, or confusion arising from regional differences regarding weight, the authoritative standard established by tradition is stated:

Not only by way of its form, but also by way of its measure, this much alone is to be given; nothing more, because the purpose would be exceeded,
meaning that the perfection of silence [would be lost].
In this context, "clinging to the earth" (bhūsparśa) means "clinging to the tip" (koṭakālagaṇaṃ) in the sense of giving.
(293) It becomes constant for one who has been entreated.

they should not, because of such a request, allow one who is unworthy to go forth or grant him full ordination.
"This is done so that one does not transgress such rules as: 'One should not go without a bowl during the rainy season.'"
In the same way, there is a pentad.

Since one should not grant the going forth even without a water-strainer and a sitting mat, these three [are required].
Therefore, it should be understood that this [requirement] has been established.
(295-296-297) During the rainy season, one should not be without a bowl.
He should not go wandering through the countryside.
He traveled with a wicked companion in a state of fear.
Upananda had ordained one who was unworthy;
while traveling through the countryside together with the monks, he arrived at a small town.
There, the monks were invited by a householder for a meal; however,
that newly ordained monk had no alms-bowl.
That householder complained, and the Blessed One said: "A monk must not travel through the countryside without an alms-bowl.
[The monks] were robbed by those who take what is not given; the Blessed One said: "A spare bowl should be carried."
"The bowl should be set aside; during the rainy season, the bowl should be kept ready"—this is the text regarding this matter.
(298-299-300) One should not allow [a person] to go forth in the absence [of these].
One should not, while standing, drag the bowl,
throw it down, or dry it.
One should consume [food] in moderation.
To demonstrate that enjoyment, he says:
(301) One should not discharge it here with anything else.
"With anything else" means with another vessel.
"Discharge" refers to that which has the nature of being cast away.

"One should not abandon the boat" is what continues [from the previous rule].

A novice monk who is subject to negligence should not adorn himself.
Nor with cow dung mixed with sand.
One should not extinguish it while it is too wet;

and one should not place it upon a stone.
This establishment is for that duration only.
(309) Not in an impure place.

The term "region" (pradeśa) continues [to apply], as does "establishment" (sthāpana).

This prohibition is for the purpose of not overstepping [the time limit] anywhere,
not for the sake of that specific time itself.

For the purpose of placing the bowl.
"Mālakam" is the name for a window. To explain how it is constructed, he says:

(314) [The meat] of the cakoraka bird [is fit for consumption] with forest-dwellers.
The implement for placing the bowl (pātrasthāpanārthakaraṇa). Regarding its common usage under the alternative reading *ākāśamālaka*, he asks: "Of what material is it made?"—and says:
(315) "Of that which consists of creepers" or "of the rope"; the meaning is "of that which is made of rope," namely, a product.
(316) For one who has been smeared, [the purification is] with cow-dung and earth.
(317) [This refers to] that which possesses such a covering.
The meaning is that its lid, whether made of creeper or rope, should also be smeared with cow-dung and clay.

There is no placing it on the ground.

The bowl.

Thus, having given the ālayanaka for the leading of the bowl (pātra).

The meaning is that in one [mouth] there is a vessel, in another medicine, and in another a lethal poison.
Furthermore, *kolāhala* refers to substances such as *ārā*, *vadhrikā*, and so forth.
(326) He should bear this sin.
Thus end the sections concerning the bowl and other requisites.

The meaning is that in these small containers (*vikā*) situated within the bowls (*pātra*) and so forth, the *ālayanaka* should not be given to those whose objects of focus (*ālambana*) are of equal strength.
And thus, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*) is: "Noble one, what is this drum? (*mṛdaṅga*)?
Therefore, this [statement] is intended to negate the utility of a simultaneous application.

In which place is there no voting? He says:

It is in the midst of this [assembly] of distinct individuals.

And the remaining robe-cloth.

Binding, cooking, washing, sprinkling, and dyeing—

Because of the arising from reality:
that whose arising occurs as a mere vessel within the reality of that state,
and whose production occurs precisely through its having become that.

To the question, "Does this belong to this one alone? he says: "No."
(355) Or [it is] because of the arising of reality, like that of a potsherd.
"Establishment" (upasthāpana) refers to the connection;

Having filled it with ashes, one should properly perform the breaking [of the vessel] with a jar-breaker.

Of the one who breaks the jar.

By means of water, [the bowl] belongs to the neighboring [monastery] itself.

from a monk who is engaged in that purpose, who is devoted to the Teaching, and who is virtuous, as he departs from his monastery room which contains his requisites and while he is on the path toward it;
