—the robe, the sitting mat, and the bowl; these are the five.
And for one who has received full ordination.
One should be constantly bound to the five requisites;
one should not be harsh like a lion.
They should not engage in any activity that results in distress.
The monks have become the Saṃgha.
(422) Paliguddhatā is the state of the mouth being parched.

This explains that it is improper to perform the destruction [of impurities], or to rise from one's night-quarters with a tooth-stick or another object in the mouth, or to pay homage to one’s preceptor or another, or to consume food. This is the demonstration of that point.

"A monk must not consume alms-food without having discarded his tooth-stick; if he does so, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*sātisāra*). This refers to what was stated in the context of the *vastu* (subject matter) concerning the immediate sequence [of rules]: "Consuming food that has not been formally offered and that has been stored constitutes a rejection [of the rule]."
"Without having understood the essential meaning, you are overstepping by treating [the subject] as a mere matter of food";
such is the demonstration of this point.

In the *Niśrayavṛtti*, it is stated here: “The co-resident or the pupil, having risen early in the morning, having put on the lower robe and wrapped [the upper robe] properly, and having discarded the tooth-stick, performs the worship of the shrine within the boundary,” and so forth; the statement that the purification of the mouth occurs by discarding this tooth-stick is found in this very passage.
Therefore, this is the sūtra: //
(423) One should discard the tooth-stick. This [practice of discarding it] is not fitting;
therefore, its purpose is to serve as a support for cleansing the mouth.
He explains how one should respond: "How should one answer? he says.
(424) It is indeed concealed.
(425) And the activity of excreting feces and urine.
It is indeed concealed.
(426) Nor at the end of that which is to be enjoyed, such as a tree or a wall.
The word "ante" means "nearby";
the meaning is that where a great crowd of people always resides is a place for enjoyment, and one should not perform acts such as discarding tooth-sticks there.
(427) Its measurement begins from twelve finger-breadths and extends up to eight.
The word *asya* refers to the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
In this reading, *ā-aṣaṭakāt*, there is a sandhi; the meaning is that its measurement begins from twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) and extends down to eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*).
(428) Up to four times more than that, in the case of one with an abundance of phlegm, [the dose] is absent.
The measurement immediately following that which exceeds four finger-breadths, up to that limit,
is the measure for a tooth-stick for one with much phlegm. (VinSū 43)

In this text it says: "In this context, 'in between' means in the middle; however, those who have an abundance of phlegm should discard their tooth-stick after removing a length of four finger-breadths."
(429) It is not improper to discharge [waste] upon a clod of earth in a latrine.
Because "of the dismissal" (*visarjanasya*) is the subject under discussion, it refers to the dismissal of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
(430) There is no lack of attainment here, because the protection occurs through the gateway of the conduit.
In this context, regarding the discarding of the tooth-stick, the meaning is that concealment—namely, being hidden—is indeed accomplished at the mouth of the conduit.
In this case, such a thing as the *hastasāmantaka* is possible.
"Herein" means at the opening of the indirect method (*praṇāḍīmukha*).
"Of such a kind" refers to that which is of the same category as the discarding of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), such as the washing of the feet and so forth, which are to be performed.
The meaning is that the possibility [of the action] pertains to the vicinity of the hand; one should not perform the discarding of the tooth-stick and so forth beyond the vicinity of the hand.
(432) He should scrape his tongue after [the brushing].
"Of him" refers to the one who has discarded the tooth-stick.
(433) He should keep a tongue-scraper ready. (434) [He should also keep] needle and thread.
A needle-shaped cavity is made of silver, copper, iron, or bell-metal; that is to say, it is made of materials having those respective forms.
In this context, a split piece of tooth-stick wood is appropriate for this purpose.
"In this matter" means for the purpose of licking the tongue clean.
(436) Boldness is for the sake of mutual non-aggressiveness toward her.
"Mutually" means one another;
"of this" refers to the split piece of tooth-stick.
One should not rub one's teeth, tongue, or ears with a sharp object.
Not quickly; the meaning is that one should rub it gently.
Not obstructing the flesh.
Thus ends the section on the gums and teeth.
(440) One should not spit out the air from between the teeth and tongue without first washing the region smeared with food-remnants or without covering it with dust.
This is connected with the phrase "one should discard the cleansing of the tooth-stick.
In the absence of water, or without rinsing [the mouth] with dust, one should discard the cleansing of the teeth and tongue;
furthermore, "cleansing" refers respectively to the tooth-stick and the fibrous brush for these two.
(441) It cannot be designated.
As it has been said: "One should cast away the dyad."
(442) This is an illustration.
The meaning is that by the mention of "cleansing" (viśabdana), the cleaning of the teeth and tongue is implied, as well as other [related acts] implied by this;
he shows what is implied by the illustration: //
(443) Even excrement, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, vomit, and purgings, as well as other such things.
It becomes something like excrement when vomited,
or something like feces when purged—
as, for example, in the case of one suffering from nasal discharge or diarrhea.

Just as in the case of the emission of yellow bile (*pīta*), even though it is designated as excrement or phlegm (*kheṭa*), there is the specific mention of "vomited" and "purged. This is for the purpose of including everything that exceeds [the normal state] among things such as excrement; furthermore, the expression "and so forth" (*iti*) is used for this reason.
(444) For this reason also, there is the perfection of humbling pride.
Even from cow dung that has been dried in the morning.
Thus, from the relinquishing of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*),
there is also success through cow-dung (*gomaya*) and *uṣāṭuka*:
"In the absence of a tooth-stick, the mouth should be cleansed with cow-dung and *uṣāṭuka*"— this is the text on this point.
(445) One should pay homage to the caitya immediately after performing one's bodily duties.
Following the discarding of the tooth-stick, whatever duties are to be performed—therefore:
(a) The practice based on reliance (niśritapratipad).
Now, the practice based on reliance:
The word "atha" (now/then) has the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*), not the sense of immediate succession (*anantarya*).
From this point forward, the practice based on reliance (*niśrita-pratipad*) is to be understood as the subject under discussion.
Immediately after this, having approached in the morning, one should perform prostration.
Therefore, "from this" means from the performance of bodily duties subsequent to the veneration of the *caityas*.

Since the performance of bodily duties for one who is dependent occurs when he is healthy at dawn, it should be understood that [the veneration] of the dependent [preceptor] takes place even earlier than that.
Because one who has a purified mouth should be desired as foremost in paying homage;
otherwise, for one who is dependent [on such purity], there arises an obstacle.
Nor should it be thought that this contradicts the instruction regarding the offering of a tooth-stick with its tip intact.
Because there is the presence of an opportunity in cases such as illness.
(448) Inquiring after one's welfare.
(449) The offering of a tooth-stick made of *uṣāṭuka* wood.
Having looked toward the kitchen, he made this announcement.
Thus, regarding that after-drink which was prepared there for the announcement—
(451) The mental attention consisting in regarding what is pleasant as something to be offered.
When this has been announced, the mental attention is as follows: "I shall present this to that beloved one toward whom he displays affection, saying, 'This is for him.'"
(452) Washing the alms-bowl.
If the śrāvaka is firmly resolved to be a mendicant who lives on alms-food, [he should practice thus].
The cleansing of that which is called by the second name "Ravakṣaraka": it is a "rāvaka" because it makes the sound "rai."
(454) If it were accompanied by a purposeful motive, then even the act of pouring out [the water] would be [a valid action].
The connection is with the term "devoid of pride" (*nirmādana*).
Furthermore, the purpose is that sometimes one must eat outside;
if that occurs, it should also be asked.
If that too is a question.
He is one who lives on alms;
therefore, for the purpose of entering for alms-food, there is an inquiry regarding what is pleasing to him, by way of entering with or without assistance.
(456) If it is argued that there is assistance—
When the support enters together with that which is supported.
—It is agreed that entry shall take place together with that very same preceptor.
(457) In the case of uneven terrain and the like, one should proceed ahead.
(458) And the dedication of that which is sublime to him.
If excellent alms-food is obtained, it should be dedicated to him [with the thought]: "Give this to us."
(459) If [it is argued that it is] incapable—
Thus is the entry.
—having arrived, [he gave] a demonstration.
Thus it is for Piṇḍaka. If one asks, "In what manner should it be dedicated?"—
(460) Regarding the presentation of the most excellent [food]: whatever highly flavorful food and drink is there, it should be presented for his support with the words, "Please accept this."
He should be moderate in all things.
Thus is the basis.
(462–463) A water vessel filled with water.
The announcement of the time.
Thus concludes the section on the time for eating.
(464) After eating, one should wash the bowl and other utensils.
(465) This is its establishment.
Of a bowl or similar object that has been polished.
(466–471) Regarding the veneration of a *caitya*, there is the presentation of flowers, incense, water, and so forth.
The performance of the rite pertaining to the washing of the feet.
The preparation of beds and seats.
The offering of the lower garment;
the taking of the lower garment.
The presentation of a foot-washing stand and a basin for the water used for washing the feet.
The word "pāda" (foot) is connected individually with both "udaka" (water) and "adhiṣṭhāna" (base/support).
It refers to the offering of foot-baths and foot-rests made of bricks.
(472-274) Wiping off the footwear.
Seeing one who has been appointed as the one who raises [the broom] but has taken up the broom for sweeping, one should show little enthusiasm.
And having accepted a needle, he was not appointed as a robe-maker.
"Having seen [this], one should make [the other] less concerned"— this is the rule.
However, if he is agreed upon as the one who performs the rising [to assist] or as the attendant for the robes, there is no fault in not making him less concerned.

(475) Even the preparation of [water] for ritual use, the gathering of small amounts of green vegetables, the collecting of flowers and fruits, and the procuring of tooth-sticks are also [prohibited] for a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśa*).
The meaning of "what is to be done with respect to the basis" is understood from the context;
and by the word "also," everything previously mentioned is included.
Furthermore, regarding the necessity of acting within the Saṃgha, one should proceed according to the principle that "this is what must be done by him."
(476) By striking the door-bolt, one should awaken those staying inside.
And another monk as a formal support;
this is the procedure for all matters involving legal disputes.
(477) This [should be done] slowly.
The striking of the city gates.
(478) He does not transgress the proper time.
Thus, the meaning is that one should not strike it repeatedly with a hammer,
nor indeed should one pierce it.
(479) One should not press [it] with excessive force.
The meaning is that one should not throw this bolt, known as the "second door," with excessive force.
(480) Knowing [the time], he should enter and exit slowly, without jostling the two door-panels.
The meaning is that it is so that no boldness arises in others.
(481) One should honor him.
"Enam" refers to the basis (*niśraya*).
Since the context concerning the basis and that which depends upon the basis remains uninterrupted throughout the intervening section, the word "enam" serves to refer back to the basis.
(482) It would adhere.
The word "this" is to be supplied [from the previous context];
the meaning is that one should dwell in close association with the support (niśraya) and not remain at a distance from it.
(483) It is not contradictory to that.
The suffix "-ālīyeta" means "to adhere";
the meaning is that one should not cling to that which is contrary to reliance.
(484) One should feel shame on account of this.
"Therefore" means by way of reliance;
what is meant is that one should possess a sense of shame.
(485) He should be skillful in his duties.
Dakṣa means not indolent;
this is the basis for it.
(486) One who acts with reverence.
The meaning is that whatever is to be done by him must be performed once and for all.
(487) One whose setting forth is graceful.
He is endowed with graceful deportment, such as the manner of approaching and so forth.

(488) "Possessing shame" means having respect (*sagaurava*). Although respect is a specific form of shame, nevertheless, because this [term] does not derive its meaning from that word, it is mentioned separately.
Shame (hrī) is the contraction of one's outward expansion.
(489) "One who is respectful."
Respectfulness is a specific form of moral dread (*apatrāpya*) characterized by the awareness of being dependent on others.
(490) One whose mind is base.
One whose pride has been destroyed.
(491) Fully aware and not neglecting his own duty.
Meditation, study, and so forth.
(492) Or, when seeking what is wholesome regarding a task to be done?

One who has taken refuge in this [teaching], whether by asking questions, giving to attendants and so forth, or by relying on others, should be one who seeks what is wholesome; the meaning is that one should not be intent on worldly affairs (*lokayātrā*), but should perform this [practice].
One should prevent [others] from falling into a state of transformation (*vikriyā*).
If that support should undergo any change,
it must be restrained by the one who relies upon it.
(494) If there is no increase in merit elsewhere, one should request that [the merit] be transferred to someone else who performs such deeds.
If, while relying on that support, his wholesome qualities do not increase,
then he should request to be entrusted with another support that causes the increase of wholesome qualities.
Having ascertained him through questioning and other means, he too should entrust him to one who is fit to provide guidance.
Furthermore, there is that which must be done by one who relies upon a support.
(496–498) Warding off evil friends.
Application to what is wholesome.
Its summary.
The meaning is the bringing about of the wholesome.
(499) Effort should be made toward the restoration from an offense and toward the attainment of the requisites of life that are conducive [to such restoration]. (VinSū 46)

Just as these two qualities are accomplished for one who is dependent, so too should effort be exerted toward the support with the thought, "May he also do this for me. Thus, based on the *Catuḥ-atikrānta-sūtra*, it should be understood that even by one who is dependent, effort must be made for the support to achieve these two qualities.

(500) A co-resident, a pupil, a preceptor, a teacher, a fellow-preceptor, a fellow-teacher, one with whom one converses, one with whom one chats, one who is well-acquainted, or one who is affectionate, should attend to a sick person.

For one who is called "ālaptaka" (one with whom one has conversed) is someone brought to a state of affection through the practice of pleasant conversation and so forth; a "saṃlaptaka" (one with whom one has discussed) is one with whom this person of confidence engages in conversation from time to time.

One who is "intimately acquainted" is so because, through traveling together to the same place and other such activities, a state of mutual physical and emotional integration has arisen with that person.
One who is "affectionate" is so because, upon seeing or hearing [the person], mere joy arises even in the absence of such physical integration.
(501) In the absence of a prior action, there is a subsequent one.

In the absence of the preceding person among the co-resident disciples (sārdhavihārī), the resident pupils (antevāsī), and so forth, each subsequent one should attend upon him. In the absence of the co-resident disciple performing attendance, the resident pupil should attend; by him, the preceptor (upādhyāya) [is served].
"Therefore, 'the teacher' and so forth:
because of the superior status of the preceptor (upādhyāya), the state of being an Arhat belongs first to those two preceding him; and from the teacher (ācārya) [comes it] for the resident disciple."
From his co-resident disciple and from his resident pupil; and because of being closer [to him], the first [of the two] who was previously struck attained Arhatship first.
(502) Here, the recitation teacher is also included.
And by the mention of "the Teacher" (ācārya) [in this context].
(503) It is that by which activity proceeds when one is dependent on another due to being unable to provide assistance.
"Sāhya" refers to the state of being weary, which is to be attended to in various ways.

"In the case of incapacity" means that if one is unable to attend from even one side, then one should attend by relying [on another]; as to what that reliance is, he says: "by which there is activity."
One should perform what is to be done after having consulted [the preceptor].
In the interim, whenever someone commits an offense against another, one should then proceed with that matter toward that person.
In the event of a transgression by those who cause harm, one should depart, having abandoned everything; this is the meaning.
(504) Here, one who has assumed the outward signs of that [state] is like a renunciant.
In this context, regarding the subject of attending to the sick,

one who has been provided with the mere outward appearance through shaving the head and so forth for the sake of renunciation, but has not yet actually been ordained, should be regarded as if he were an ordained monk.
The meaning is that one should attend to him when he is ill in the same manner as one attends to a renunciant.
(505) They should not neglect a fellow practitioner who is ill.
(506) In his absence, they should provide him with an attendant until the end.
"In his absence" means in the absence of one who dwells together with him and so forth.
To the question "Until when should it be given?", he says: "until the end."
If, even with one who has been given, there is still a lack of an attendant, then others should be given because of the inability to fulfill the requirement due to the absence of such a person;
this continues until the limit of the Saṃgha is reached— this is the meaning.

“When there is a lack of everyone, the Saṃgha, having determined the state of the illness, should assign attendants—one, two, or many; at the very least, the entire Saṃgha must provide nursing care. This is the textual passage here.
[Because of the reliance on medicine—
] it is permissible for a sick person alone to consume medicine from the Saṅgha.
Whatever medicine belongs to the householder Muṇḍa should be placed in the communal infirmary for the Saṅgha;
it is to be consumed by the sick monks—thus is its inclusion herein. (VinSū 47)
(508) If [the person] is not a sentient being, one should encourage the one who established [the precept] to undertake it.
When such an absence exists, this should be undertaken by one who establishes it.
(509) In the event that they cannot be obtained, they should give what belongs to the Saṃgha.
If, even when being exhorted, he does not comply, then the meaning is that what belongs to the Saṃgha must be given to him.
(510) In the absence of [an offense] pertaining to the Saṃgha,
it is a mental offense arising from that which pertains to the body.

Even that which is already fastened upon a statue or in a shrine, such as ornaments and so forth—up to whatever may be given—if there is nothing else, what more need be said regarding other things? This is the meaning.
(511) They should perform acts such as offering drinks and erecting parasols for his sake [from the communal funds].
The phrase "in the absence" carries over; in the absence of one's own [property], it belongs to the Saṃgha. "Of this" means of that which belongs to the Saṃgha. (512)
In the absence of this [wealth], it should be given from one's intellectual property; if one is afflicted by these two [diseases] and possesses wealth, it should be given even at the risk of death.
"By these two" means by those belonging to the Saṅgha and those belonging to the Buddha;
however, if there is no gift, there is an absence of fault.
(514) No attendant should wait upon him.
"Enam" refers to one who is ill.
One should not oppose his command, which is both beneficial and righteous.
"Beneficial" means connected with the vessel of life;
"of this one" refers to the sick person;
"righteous" means connected with the service of merit.
(516) One should not maintain a state of attachment toward an object that has been requested.
The object of attachment is that bowl or other item for which the sick person has a craving;
"upayācita" refers to the attendant [who provides it] for the sake of the sick person.
(517) "One should not instruct [them]."
An attendant for the sick.
(519) A sick person should not overstep this: the meaning is that a sick person should not disregard the instruction given by an attendant.
(519) That attendant, upon perceiving a danger of death for him, should raise him from the communal bedding and seating and settle him in a private dwelling.
(520) By way of the pretext of [requiring] anointing and bathing.
The meaning is that one should cause [the object] to enter by means of the pretext consisting of anointing and bathing;
since the pretext is the primary factor here,
these two should be understood as illustrations.
(521) One should be diligent in discerning that state.
This means that one should be diligent in discerning the state of death—that is, in whatever bodily state there arises a suspicion of death. And "diligence" here refers to repeated examination.
(522) Its being an effect of that [is] the washing of the robes of those who have died from the afflictions produced by that.

Regarding "the robes of those who have been defiled by that sick person having died": if those robes belong specifically to the one who was the attendant of that sick person and who has now died, and not to anyone else, then they are to be washed.
The meaning is that this is what must be done by that attendant.
(523) That elder should be the first to take his place in the assembly of the Saṃgha.
This refers to the manner in which these [monks] rely upon their support; within this context, there is the introduction of the authority of the senior monk (sthavira) of the Saṃgha.
The meaning is that when the Saṃgha is assembled, the senior monk of the Saṃgha should be the one who takes the lead.
(524) One should wait for a delay in departure.
Therefore, he is an elder (sthavira).
(525) "They too [will wait for him]" means that those for whom he is an elder will also wait for him as he delays his departure.
(526) And though it has not gone out, it has traveled far.
(527) And [the rule applies] at the edge of a village;
here, the word *anta* signifies proximity.
(528) If there is entry here, it follows that which is following after.

If entry is intended, they should wait for him as he approaches at the edge of the village. While they are waiting—if there should be a messenger [they should say]: "Wait, Venerable One, until... (VinSū 48)
They should say, "He is coming."
"Enam" refers to the messenger.
And when the giving of water with the hand has been performed for the purpose of eating, if there is still time remaining.

When they have arrived for the sake of food or drink, at the time of offering water with the hands, if there is time while they are waiting, then they should say to this messenger: "Wait until the senior of the Saṃgha arrives."
(531) If this instruction were not present here, they would abandon their posture.
If the time for the formal inspection has not yet arrived, the seat of the senior of the Saṃgha must be vacated when sitting down for the meal or other activities.
While seated, he should also look outward and reflect.
He is seated within the house, that is, outside of the hermitage grounds.
The senior monk of the Saṃgha must perform an inspection regarding these two states.
This is for the purpose that no one here may be poorly clothed or unclothed.
(533) If it is difficult to cover or difficult to dress, one should provide a remedy for these two in order to achieve excellence.
"Of these two" refers to being poorly covered and being poorly dressed.
"The cause for him" refers to that which is poorly covered or poorly dressed.
(534) In the case of non-penetration, one should cause it to be performed immediately thereafter.
If he, being poorly dressed, does not perceive the signal being made by the senior of the Saṃgha, then the one who is next in rank to him should have it done.
(535) In the case of non-attainment, [the result arises] spontaneously.
Even so, if the cause of excellence is not achieved, he should have it done himself;
if the sign is not perceived, he should have it done by means of verbal instruction.
(536) He should not converse with those novices who are there, [thinking], "He is the senior of the Saṃgha there."
(537) Wherever their conduct in monasteries and forests is appropriate, one should cause them to adopt that conduct [and should also enjoin them to it].
"Of those" refers to the novices (*navaka*).
"That conduct" refers to the conduct of the monastery (*vihāra-vṛtta*) and the conduct of the forest (*araṇya-vṛtta*). And "he should appoint" means:
One should not only cause them to grasp that conduct, but one must also enjoin them to the actual practice of that conduct.
(b) A later-comer monk (paścāt-śramaṇa),
being a guest, should inspect [the quarters] and inform the resident monks regarding the bedding and seating.
The senior monk of the visiting community should inspect the bedding and seating for the sake of those resident monks to whom that senior monk belongs,
and he should inform them regarding the bedding and seating.

(539) One who is traveling should set out after having weighed the directions, the caravan, the lodging, the bedding and seating, and the companions, according to their inability to provide assistance in times of illness.

The *gamika-saṃghasthavira* (the senior monk who is traveling) is so called because he must attend to the needs of those traveling. This means that he must mentally evaluate—both as to what is appropriate and inappropriate—all matters concerning the direction to be traveled, the caravan, the route, and the lodging; furthermore, regarding the bedding and seats at the destination, and in the event of illness, no one among the companions should be abandoned by anyone else.
The meaning is that, having deliberated in this manner, one should then proceed toward the attainment of the desired state.
(540) Afterwards, he should ensure that nothing whatsoever is forgotten by anyone, and having approached them closely, he should cause them to remember it clearly.
It is the senior monk of the Saṃgha himself.
(541) One should establish those who are neither agitated nor arrogant in the state of being free from arrogance.
The meaning is that one should establish oneself in the opposite of lack of tranquility, which is restlessness, and of rigidity, which is arrogance.
And all [beings], having approached, are entirely virtuous.
The phrase "he should establish them in being neither agitated nor arrogant" is to be supplied [to the preceding].
It is not only the Elder who is capable of this,
but others as well.
And it does not mean only novices, but rather others as well; such is the meaning.
(543) Be aware:
the elder of the Saṅgha is departing.

Favor him by attending to his needs, such as the communal conduct, deportment, instruction, recitation, and so forth, as well as by providing food, care during illness, and the fulfillment of all other duties.
The sphere of conduct;
the movement of the postures;
the instruction on these two.
"This is the proper domain, this is not the proper domain; one should proceed in this manner," and so forth.
In the phrase "instruction and so forth" (*uddeśādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the private recitation (*svādhyāyanika*) and other such activities.
(544) When he has entered the rains retreat, he should have the monastery repaired if it is not being repaired by those who intend to do so;
and he should encourage those who are repairing it.
(545) When all those present in the assembly desire discourse, he should favor them by providing a presentation of the Dharma that is conducive [to their needs].
If those present in the assembly seek discourse, then let him favor them with whatever application of the Dharma is appropriate for each individual.
"Everyone" refers to the elder of the Saṅgha,
and not merely the elder of the Saṅgha who has entered the rains-retreat.
(546) He should maintain equanimity toward those who delight in silence.
Silence (*tūṣṇībhāva*) means the state of being silent (*tūṣṇītva*).
Here, "noble silence" (*āryas tūṣṇīṃbhāvaḥ*) is intended, not mere muteness.
A householder should share with others the food that has been brought to him.
"It is proper to give them food.
Having informed the monks, if those monks do not share [the food] when told by the senior of the community (saṃghasthavira), or if those householders do not wish to eat, then—
(548) Or, if [the opponent] neither performs nor approves [of the argument], one should speak this discourse regarding the subject (*dharmī*), saying: "This is what we possess."
One who possesses that [knowledge] should examine the entire assembly.
The meaning is that every member of the assembly [is so], not only the elder of the Saṃgha.
One should restrain one who acts foolishly.
The phrase "everyone who possesses an assembly" is to be supplied [to each clause].
The meaning is that one should act in such a way that one does not let time pass in vain, nor does one make the going forth (pravrajyā) fruitless.
(551) Just as one would act here regarding going and so forth.
The word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to considerations regarding configuration, such as "one should walk in this way," "one should stand in this way," and so on.
"In this" refers to the assembly;
"just as this" refers to the assembly.
The meaning is: "in accordance with the assembly."
(552) He should not engage in talk about various worldly matters or about horizontal [secular] affairs.
The word "here" (atra) is understood [from the previous context].
Having departed from the Dharma and Vinaya, she moves away from his side; her discourse is lateral.
Scattered among various discourses.
A śramaṇa should not walk ahead or behind [the teacher].
"One should not remain."
The meaning is that one should not stand in front of or behind a śramaṇa.
(555) It is said that one should speak thus.
Nothing further need be said that has not already been stated.
Or he should accomplish it.
The meaning is that he should fulfill whatever is requested of him by the *puraḥśramaṇa*.
(557) One should not interrupt another's conversation.
The meaning is that while the preceding śramaṇa is engaged in conversation, one should not interrupt with another conversation.
(558) To one who speaks what is unrighteous,
he should reply thus to the preceding śramaṇa:
(559–560) One should rejoice in the Dharma.
Accept the merit-based gain that has been properly acquired.
Thus [ends the section on] the junior monk.
This is the subsequent conduct of a śramaṇa.
(c) The monk who visits families:
the conduct of one who visits families is now described.
(561) "Unstuck" (*anunnaḍaḥ*):
thus [it applies] to everyone.
In a family, one should be unstuck—that is, not fixed [in worldly attachments].
The desire to depart from the household and the state of non-settledness.
(562) With downcast eyes.
The meaning is that his eye is withdrawn from sense objects.

(VinSū 50) (564) One should employ them in acts of giving, self-restraint, self-control, living the holy life, observing the upoṣadha fast, going for refuge, and undertaking the precepts of training.

Discipline (*vinayana*) is abiding in discipline (*viniyata-avasthāna*), and living the holy life (*brahmacaryavāsa*); these constitute the conduct of one who has gone forth (*pravrajita-vṛtta*). Furthermore, for a householder, it is the lifelong abstention from vulgar practices (*grāmyadharma*).

"Mindful" means, by implication, regarding transgressions (*āpatti*).

When setting out on such actions as entering a family home, which serve as the gateway for the arising of a transgression, one should establish mindfulness in such a way that no transgression whatsoever occurs.
(566) It is not the case that there is no following after what has been taught.
The word "should practice" is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis. Since this [person] has not been instructed, he is not bound [to the practice],

The meaning is that one should not transgress his instruction.

"Come" means one who speaks words of welcome; the meaning is that one should be a speaker of pleasant words even before the initial greeting.

(570) With brows free from frowning.
(571) If a householder has a guest arrive, he should engage him in discourse concerning the Dharma.

[Thinking, "He will not come," O housewife, the village-dwelling monk should provide as much as he is able of pleasing food and so forth.]

In the *Āraṇyaka* as well,
the analysis is "water and a seat."
(574) The junior monk shall perform the sweeping, the arrangement of beds and seats, the setting out of water, the distribution [of water], and the serving of food.
In every assembly, wherever it may be, all of this must be performed by that novice.
One should undertake contrary conduct toward one's attendants, provided it does not result in harm to oneself or others.
"He should approach" means he should remain equanimous;
provided that what is being undertaken does not lead to the harm of himself or others.
If [it is said] to him— // (576) //
If that action of the attendants were for the purpose of causing harm;
If one has the capacity, having completely cut off this contrary action, one should perform another.
In accordance with the Dharma—
Action.
Having thus generated [it]— //
The retinue.
One should cause him to understand.
Whether there is destruction or no growth, the cause of that is the maintenance of the retinue.

Thus, while that righteous activity is being undertaken, if there should arise in his attendants a breakdown of spirit, dejection, or an inability to endure it, or if they depart for some other reason, he should remedy that through such means as giving;
he should act so that these two conditions do not occur among his attendants.
(578) If there is an inability [to proceed], one should depart by another way.
Thus, when it is impossible to eradicate [the fault] by oneself, one must proceed by means of another.
But one should not analyze it by taking that condition apart.
Of the retinue.
One should say.
(580) If one commits an offense within a monastic residence, one should act in such a way that one undergoes formal apprehension by means of a self-accusation.

(581) Without having informed anyone who is arriving, he should suddenly cause the prince, the friend, the minister, the official, and the royal son to seize the attendants at the feet [of the offender] and have him struck down before a pure assembly.
"Having caused [them] to grasp" means having awakened [them].
"The assembly of the pure" refers to that wherein one is not punished; therein one should strike down or defeat [the opponent], such is the meaning.
However, as for the prior awakening of youths and others, that is for this purpose: until they are defeated, one should not cause harm by relying upon them—this is the meaning.
That which pertains to the monks, connected with the section on going forth, has been explained.
(d) Concerning the nun:
that which pertains to the nun is now being explained.
In this regard, having accepted that whatever was stated concerning "a man" with respect to going forth and full ordination applies equally to a woman, the specific distinction is now explained.
(582) A bhikṣuṇī [is to be dealt with] in the place of a bhikṣu.

The meaning is that where a monk is mentioned in relation to one who has become a part of the Saṅgha or who has become [one with] it—such as one who approves of the preceptor (upādhyāya-rocaka) and so forth—there a nun is to be understood.
Does this apply to every monk, or only to some? He says: [it applies to] no one.
(583) [The same applies] to everyone regarding the going forth into homelessness.
In matters concerning ordination, for everyone including the preceptor and others, a nun must take the place of a monk.
The announcement for the sake of the female preceptor, the bestowing of the novice vow, and all such matters must be performed by the nuns alone.
There is no authority for a monk in this matter; such is the demonstration of that point.
(584) Regarding full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), [the offense] belongs to the performer of the ritual action (*karmakartṛ*) when there is a request for it by another and so forth.
In the case of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), a nun is not to be regarded as standing in the place of every monk;
rather, [she is so regarded] in the request for ordination and similar procedures.

From the moment of the request for ordination onwards, the nun who performs the ritual act (*karmakāraka*) stands in the place of a monk other than the one performing the rite; it is thus stated that in this context, the performer of the ritual is indeed a monk, not a nun.

But prior to the formal request for full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), there is the nun who acts as the officiant of the ritual (*karmakārikā*), she who bestows the restraint of the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) in the midst of the exclusive community of nuns.
(585) Here, the Saṅgha is the accuser.
In this context of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) is present at the beginning, during the request, and so forth.
It should be understood as being for the purpose of accumulation;
the meaning is that when both Saṅghas have assembled, the formal act (karman) must be performed starting from the request (yācanā).
(586) Speaking [of one's faults] in the presence of a nun may be an obstacle or something that constitutes an impediment.

Thus, regarding the proclamation of obstacles, two formal acts are performed within the midst of the Saṃgha: one is performed solely within the midst of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, while the two [formal acts] concerning the granting of the restraint for the practice of celibacy are performed within the midst of both Saṃghas.
This rule is to be understood as applying to both cases as well.
This was stated as the cause for modesty; therefore, the employment of the verb at the beginning is for the purpose of making known that one may act according to one's own will.
(587) The state of being a *śikṣamāṇā* is another stage for a woman.
The state of being a female novice and the state of being a nun— these two occasions are common to both sexes;
however, this third occasion belongs specifically to her,
and that is as follows:
(588) Only when it is dependent.

The word "even" (eva) is intended to show that there is no distinction between the state of being a female novice (śrāmaṇerikā) and the state of being a nun (bhikṣuṇī); just as these two [categories] are [distinguished],
so too is this [case].

And for this reason, one should approach a certain nun as one's preceptor (upādhyāyikā), and not that very same person who served as the preceptor for the sake of the female novice (śrāmaṇerikā); such is the practice.
Thus, there is a triad of preceptors for a woman.
In the case of a man, however, the state of being "one who has become [a trainee]" (*jāta*) arises.
At what stage does the name "trainee" (*śikṣamāṇā*) apply to a woman—another stage—and for how long is her practice? To this he says:
(589) The period for practicing the two-year [probationary] training lies between the status of a female novice (*śrāmaṇerikā*) and that of a fully ordained nun (*bhikṣuṇī*).

The undertaking of the time is the conferring of full ordination (*upasaṃpādana*) for that specific duration; it does not mean that this vow must be practiced beyond that point. Therefore, until this period is completed, one should not fail to train in this training prior to the full ordination.
Or else, one must understand that there is the destruction of this restraint.
As for when the growth of this state of being a trainee occurs, he says:
(590) This refers to the time of ordination (*upasaṃpad*) being deficient by that much, and so forth, regarding the growth [of the roots].
The beginning of the time for full ordination (upasaṃpad) is twofold for her: [first,] the state of being twenty years old for a maiden;...
The state of being twelve years old for one who has lived at home;

by that period of training, which is two years less than the time of full ordination (upasaṃpad) and so forth— that is, beginning with the time of full ordination minus those two years— this is that time, namely, the time beginning with the time of full ordination minus those two years.
This is the time for the growth of her status as a trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*):
namely, that a maiden is eighteen years old, or, having been married, she is ten years old. This is the meaning.
The text here, in the Bhikṣuṇī-vibhaṅga, states: "She who has lived as a householder for ten years, or she who has been a maiden for eighteen years—
to her, the training and the formal admission (saṃvṛti) should be granted for two years."
The specific characteristics of the time for full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), which has been accepted here, are now being explained:
(591) The twelve-year requirement for full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) is the first [condition] regarding marriage.
When she has been married— that is, when the marriage ceremony has been performed—
the twelve-year period for full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) begins from that time.
(592) Arising from giving (*dāna*). The phrase "of one training" (*śikṣamāṇatvasya*) is to be supplied as a supplement.
By what [does one arise] from giving? He says: //
By the community of nuns.
He asks "How so? and says:
(594) Training and restraint is giving.
"This [person] of such-and-such a name requests the restraint of training (śikṣāsaṃvṛti), until the Saṃgha grants the restraint of training"— this is the indicative reference to such a formula.

(595) Immediately following this is the proclamation of the training; immediately after this giving of the restraint of training follows the proclamation of the training—the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas.
In that regard, what are the six rules?
She should not set out on a journey alone;
she should not cross to the other side of a river.
One should not touch a man with that;
one should not sleep together with him in a boat-house.
One should not engage in socializing,
nor should one conceal one's faults.
Thus, these six dharmas have been proclaimed for one in training.
What are the six secondary rules?
One should not accept gold or silver;
one should not have the hair of the private parts shaved.
One should not dig the earth,
nor should one cut green grass.
One should not consume what has not been formally offered; nor should one consume what is stored for personal use.
These six secondary dharmas have been explained,
because they are to be practiced by those in training.
(596) There is no full ordination for one who has not obtained the restraint of the foundation of the holy life.
In this context, "ordination" refers to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); its "attainment" (*upasthāna*) means its production.
The "restraint for the attainment of the holy life" (*brahmacaryopasthānasaṃvṛti*) is the restraint for the sake of attaining that holy life.
That [vow] by which she was not obtained— that is, this non-attainment of the formal undertaking of the religious life (*brahmacarya*)—
for her there is no full ordination (*upasaṃpad*),
because this formal undertaking is for the purpose of full ordination.
Because there is a restriction regarding the status of the field (*kṣetra*), one who has not obtained the objective in this [status] does not receive full ordination (*upasaṃpad*).
When is its bestowal? (597)
That gift follows after the instruction on seclusion.
The giving of that restraint which consists in the practice of the holy life.
He asks, "By what? and says:
(598) By the Saṃgha.
Because it is the subject at hand, the practice is performed by the community of nuns.
What is the nature of this gift? He says: //
(599) Having asked whether there are any obstructing factors.
Thus, there are three intermediate questions regarding this:

the first is with a nun who acts as a private instructor; the second is within the community of nuns alone, consisting of the constituent factors for the undertaking of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

The third [case] concerns the full ordination requested before both Saṃghas; it is that which constitutes a factor of the full ordination. Here, "requesting" means having made the request; from this, the undertaking of the ritual action (*karmādāna*) is obtained.
Therefore, even in this case, giving is appropriate only when [the recipient] has requested it; thus he says:
(600) Regarding the phrase "when requested":
The meaning is that the granting of this vow of undertaking the holy life occurs when it has been requested, not when it has not been requested.
(601) The fivefold [rule] regarding robes.
A nun has three robes, a waist-cloth, and a side-covering cloth; anything beyond these is an excess.
(602) Among the reliances, the state of having the roots of desire for existence as their basis.
The state of being devoid of dwelling at the foot of a tree; having abandoned the foot of a tree, there are three other supports for her.
(603) There are eight [offenses] among those involving defeat.
"Contact, confinement in a cage, covering, and warding off"—these are four additional [factors].
(604) Proclaiming the qualities of the teacher.
The eight weighty rules (gurudharma) must be proclaimed.
They are as follows: "Full ordination (upasaṃpad) is to be received from the monks; and one must seek instruction on the counteractive practices."
One should not enter the rains retreat in a residence where there are no monks, nor anywhere else whatsoever.
Exhorting a monk who has committed an offense,
not being angry, and paying homage to one who is junior.
The *mānāpya* from both groups, and the invitation (*pravāraṇā*); these are the heavy rules (*gurudharma*).
He states at what time that announcement was made: //
(605) In the interval between the acts that cause a monk to fall [from his status].
(606) [The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] before the six suffixes beginning with *kṛt*.

Regarding the phrase "one who has previously gone forth"—this means that one who possesses knowledge [of this rule], from the point "as far as" up to "do not," should ask the one who has approached for the sake of going forth, "Are you [such a person? and the ordainers should neither let her go forth nor let her be ordained; this is the meaning of what must be practiced.
And it has no nature of sprouting again.
And here, this set of six injunctions is to be understood.
The phrase "the destruction of such a person wearing sectarian marks" must be stated because it applies to all [offenses];
furthermore, it should be understood as occurring "here" [in this world].
He asks: "What is that group of six? and says:
(608)–(613) Those with both sexual organs.
With distinct phonemes.
Always flowing.
Bloody.
It is occasional.
He asks: "What is this so-called 'contingent' [knowledge]? and says:—
That which has merely the indicative mark as its manifest form is called "that" (tadākhyā).
The designation "naimittikī" (the indicative) is the name given to that [speech] whose phonemes serve merely as indicators (*nimitta*).
(614) One who has previously gone forth should be asked, when she approaches for the purpose of ordination: "Are you a hermaphrodite? and so on, up to "Have you not previously gone forth?"
The principle to be understood here is that "this [seed] does not possess the nature of sprouting."
This concludes the section on the ordination of those from the minor classes and so forth, contained within the *Pravrajyāvastu*.
(vi) Pertaining to inquiry:
(a) Regarding restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*),
[it is established that] the bodies of those in the non-human realms and those of the Northern Kurus do not constitute a field for restraint.
One who has been reborn in a destiny other than the human realm,
or even within the human realm, one who belongs to the Northern Kurus—
for these, there is no restraint (saṃvara). (VinSū 54)
The meaning is that he ascends.
In the third revolution, there is no change in the phoneme.
The phrase "it is not a field for restraint" is the subsequent connection.
The meaning is that for one whose threefold repetition of the syllables occurs, their restraint does not grow.
(617) There is no destruction in the first two [moments].
The meaning is that there is no destruction of the restraint (*saṃvara*) through the first two types of transposition of syllables.
These two rules are observed [to apply] to the minor rules (*kṣudraka*) because of their similarity.
(618) Arising occurs when there is being perceived.
When there is a transformation of the phrasing while the vow is being undertaken, there is the arising of the restraint.
“If the gender of one who desires full ordination changes, it should be said whether he is ordained or unordained.”
He said: "One who has not received full ordination should be so called."
"For the full ordination of a nun must be sought from the monks; such is the state of being a nun"—this is the text on this point.
An illustration here is the transformation of the sexual characteristics of a person;
because it is even more free from doubt, there is a difference in the rule (*vidhi*) in this case.
Here, one who is observing for ordination (*upasaṃpatprekṣī*) is understood as being in the state of one who is about to receive ordination (*upasaṃpadyamāna*).
Because it is impossible for there to be a gathering of even a single monk prior to the turning back [of the assembly].
(619) In the case of the absence of a preceptor, [the same applies] to one who possesses that [quality].
"One who possesses that" means one who possesses a preceptor;
the arising of the restraint occurs even without a preceptor.
(620) Because he has not received full ordination.
Even when one has received full ordination from a preceptor, does there arise the emergence of the restraint belonging to one who possesses a preceptor?
(621) No, for one who knows [the truth], there is no loss of monkhood.
There is no invalidation of the restraint for one who has a preceptor when the recipient knows that this preceptor is not a monk, is unordained, or is ruined.
The text on this point states: "If one seeking ordination is ordained by a preceptor who is a thief-living-in-community (stainyasaṃvāsika), he is to be declared ordained."
Is he to be called "one who has not received full ordination"?
He replied: "If he knows, 'My preceptor is one who lives in communion by theft,' then he is to be called 'one who has not received full ordination.
If he does not know,"
One should say that he is fully ordained.
In this way, by a preceptor who has previously committed [an offense], and so forth.
"By one who is a householder and whose primary activity is worldly affairs, by one who is not a preceptor.
But surely, even in the absence of being a preceptor, there is the arising of the vow; so how is it that for one who knows this, the state of being a non-monk does not occur?

If it is argued that this motivation arises because one who has failed understands that his intention was such that he was unassailable in his virtue, or that there was no harm through his virtue, that is not so.
He does not fail to recognize the state of being without a preceptor, and so forth; therefore, there is no contradiction here regarding the non-arising [of the offense].
As for that which was stated regarding the arising of the restraint when the preceptor has not been fully ordained— that refers to the Saṅgha;
the arising occurs when one knows the Saṅgha to be unordained,
not when one is looking toward full ordination.
(622) One does not reject him.
Because the preceptor is the gateway to the restraint, if one rejects him, there is no arising of the restraint.
The text here [poses the question]: "When one who is undergoing full ordination rejects the preceptor, should he be said to have been ordained or should he be said not to have been ordained?
He replied: "He should be said not to have been ordained."
(623) There is no non-manifestation of the names of these two.
If the name of either this field or this preceptor is not proclaimed by the one who undertakes [the vow], or by the agent of the ritual action, there is no arising of the restraint (*saṃvara*).
(624) Nor does it belong to the Saṅgha, because it has that as its source.
If neither the one who causes the undertaking nor the one who performs the action mentions the name of the Saṃgha,
then it arises from that source—
that is, it arises from the source of the Saṃgha.
For that lineage,
there is no arising of restraint.
The text here states: "Regarding the one who receives [the precepts], there are three types of persons who have not been fully ordained:
one who does not announce his own name;..."
"He does not state the name of his preceptor, nor does he know his full ordination"—
this passage refers to the officiant of the ritual: "He does not proclaim the names of three persons— the preceptor..."
[He] desires full ordination;
[he is] for the Saṃgha as well.
It should be said that he has been fully ordained.
"One who is not fully ordained should be so addressed" [he said—
"one who is not fully ordained should be so addressed"]. This is not a formal act of installation.
In this context, the recitation of the name of the one who receives [the precepts] is for the purpose of his own undertaking;
the presentation of the name of the Saṅgha is for the purpose of its being favored by him.

That which is not performed because the object of the action has been brought [to the officiant] by the ritual assistant (*karmakāraka*) for the sake of his taking it up; that which is not performed because the community (*saṃgha*) has been brought [to the officiant] for the sake of its being the agent of the rite;
and that which consists in the non-proclamation of the name by the ritual assistant to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
That too is a non-performance because it brings about the very fact that the Saṃgha is the agent;
for wherever there is the recognition of the Saṃgha’s agency in an action, the performance of that action belongs to someone other than it.

That which is the non-mentioning of the preceptor’s name by the one who undertakes [the vow] pertains to that action which is performed together with the preceptor; it does not present itself there as an object for him.
The non-arising of these [transgressions] occurs when their names are not brought to mind; this is the restraint.
(625) Nor [should one dwell] under the banner of householders or of non-Buddhist sectarians.
The word *dhvaja* (banner) is completed with each [term].

In the expressions *āgārikadhvaje* and *tīrthikadhvaje*, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi*. That is to say, it refers to one for whom the banner of a householder (*āgārikadhvaja*) is his banner, or one for whom the banner of a non-Buddhist ascetic (*tīrthikadhvaja*) is his banner.
He whose banner is the banner of the non-Buddhist outsiders—
when these two banners are taken up, there is no arising of restraint;
and here, "banner" refers to dress.
(626) Nor [should one eat] from naked, angry, or *puṃphālinī* women.
The phrase "the arising of the restraint" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
By the very expression "the sectarian banner of one who has become naked through formal undertaking," [the case of] nudity for other purposes is already included;
thus, the mention of "nakedness" here is for another purpose.
In this state, because the mind has abandoned its firm grasp, there is no arising of restraint (*saṃvara*);
when it is agitated, stability is destroyed.
To that extent, O Venerable Ones, they confer full ordination upon one who is like a blooming flower.
"Should she be said to be fully ordained or unordained?
[He replied: "She should be said to be unordained;
furthermore, those who performed the ordination are guilty of an offense."
When a man dies due to contact with a *puṃphālinī* in front of him, [he is reborn as such].
(627) There is no reversal of the formal act for one who has been suspended if the [required] signs are not accepted.

For one whose intention is to desist from [wrong] views, there is the accomplishment of restraint; therefore, when the cause by which an act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) is performed— such as the failure to see an offense (*āpattyadarśana*) and so forth—
is not accepted in its opposite form, there is no arising of restraint.
The case of the *utkṣiptaka* (one who has been suspended) is merely an illustration;
this same rule applies to all those who have made a formal vow [of exclusion].
This is because even one whose intention is to cause quarrels and the like possesses an intention that is not free from [the defilements].
(628) Regarding the mere *duṣkṛta* offense on Mount Apūrvaparvata:
when one enters the state of a *śrāmaṇera* without having [previously] become a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
or when one enters the state of a *bhikṣu* without having [previously] been a *śrāmaṇera*, it constitutes a mere *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no failure to undertake restraint.
The text on this point is as follows: "They confer full ordination upon one who is a householder and not a renunciant;
should he be said to be fully ordained or not fully ordained? He replied: "He is fully ordained, Upāli."
"And those who confer full ordination incur an offense of wrongdoing."
(629–630) When a preceptor asks about an obstacle during a formal request, [if one answers] falsely.
In both cases here, there is merely a transgression; there is no non-arising of the restraint— this is the underlying principle.
(631) In the case of promising this non-existent thing, there is the giving [of what is not].
Regarding "of what is non-existent" (asataḥ), that is, of something not currently present;

when one who has undertaken [the precepts] makes a claim regarding an obstructive factor— thinking "I have an obstructive factor"— there is merely a minor offense (duṣkṛta) in the granting of the restraint, but it is not a failure to undertake [the vow].

In this regard, the text in the *Nidāna* states: "Venerable Sir, they confer full ordination upon one who possesses obstructive factors (*antarāyika-dharma*), saying, 'He possesses them; he does exist [as such].
Should he be said to be ordained, or should he be said to be unordained?"
He said: "I am ordained, but those who performed the ordination are guilty of an offense.
In this context, that which is intended as an obstacle remains established;
for in such a manner was I ordained.
(632) A woman’s imitation of a man,
or a man’s imitation of a woman, constitutes a different kind of *vyañjana* offense.
There is no non-arising of the restraint here;
this is shown because, since it is a variety of a different phoneme, there would be no arising [of the offense] in this case.
And this does not occur for him.
(b) Being projected.
(633) Its implication is shown by the mention of "those with severed hands" and so forth.

For this person who possesses the quality of being an imitation, the implication is made through the phrase "those with severed hands, those with severed feet," and so on; and because of this implication, it is stated that they are merely evildoers.
(634) Of one who has conquered another continent within a world-system divided by the characteristics of evil.
The meaning is that even these two are included by such cases as "one whose hand has been cut off," and so forth.

“They confer the full ordination upon one characterized by evil”—up to this point, he is to be called "fully ordained"; however, the monks who perform the ordination incur a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is the textual passage concerning one characterized by evil (*pāpalakṣaṇa*).
Even a text from another region [of the *Nidāna*] states: "Monks from Jambudvīpa confer full ordination upon one from Pūrvavideha;
he who has been ordained should be told: '... [and so on] ... you are fully ordained, Upāli.
But those who perform the ordination are guilty of an offense."
Thus, one should compose the summary of the wheel in detail.
Where among humans there is a difference in shape, size, and condition on a particular continent, the term "continent" (*dvīpa*) is established here as a restriction to that specific measure alone.
Here, by the inclusion of the term "different [types of] kalpas," even the difference in features such as the face and so forth is intended as a difference in *kalpa*.
And thus, it should be understood that for those belonging to a single continent, this [difference] regarding the covering of the face, ears, and so forth is excluded.

(635) [They are excluded] from those with a single toenail, those with lines on the palms, those with hair on the shoulders, those with matted hair, those who are hunchbacked internally and externally, those with six [extra] fingers, those lacking fingers, those with eyelashes like a mongoose, those with eyes like a *kiṃpila* fruit, those with inverted eyes, those with closed eyes, those with eyes that are too large, those with leprosy, ringworm, or scabies, those who are yellow, white, or red, those with veins showing, those with itchy ears, those with goiters, those with thick scabies, those with deformed limbs, those with tails, those who are covered [in deformities], those who are dull-witted, those who are tongueless, those with one hand or foot, those without hands or feet, those with blue hair, and those with arms, heads, or necks as long as a palm tree, or those whose gait is impaired by disease.
And by one who is ill, [the confession] of the others.
The meaning is that those with deformed nails and so forth are included under the category of "those with severed hands" and the like;
whereas others who are afflicted by disease are included under the category of "the sick," as indicated by the phrase, "May you not be sick."
Ekanakha is one who has but a single nail;
Samudralekha is one whose bodily parts bear lines like those on a seal.
*Pakṣahetu*: one whose one side is withered;
*liṅgaśiras*: one whose head has the shape of a phallus; *gulmakeśa*: one whose hair grows in clumps. (VinSū 57)
The hair of this man stands like that of Vidūṣaka, with an inner fringe;
the term *kubja* (humpbacked) is to be applied to each [part], meaning he is humpbacked both internally and externally.
"Bent within, bent without, bent both within and without"—
this has been stated elsewhere: "one-eyed, with a withered arm," and so forth.
"Then Kubja and Vāma"— this is for the purpose of demonstrating the divisions.

In the expression "six together, [but] no fingers" (*ṣaṭ-sahitā 'naṅguli*), the word *aṅguli* (finger) is completed with each [member of the compound]. Thus, there is one who has six fingers, one whose fingers are joined together, and one who is fingerless. This constitutes the state of having six fingers.
The state of having joined fingers (*sahitāṅgulitva*) is merely the absence of [separated] fingers (*anaṅguli-tvamātraka*).
Here, the state of having stuck-together fingers (*saktāṅgulitva*) is included within the category of "fingers like a hooded hand" (*aṅguliphaṇāhastakatva*).
In the expression *pakṣma-nakula-kiṃpila-viparīta-milita-śikya-kaśmīlita-akṣākṣa*, the word *akṣa* is completed with each preceding term: *pakṣmākṣaḥ*,
*nakulākṣaḥ*,
*kiṃpilākṣaḥ*.
One with distorted eyes, one with closed eyes, and one with eyes like a scale-beam.

*Kaśmīlitākṣaḥ* means one whose eyes are squinted; *akṣākṣaḥ* means one whose eyes are [abnormal]; *pakṣmākṣaḥ* refers to one on whose eyes the eyelashes grow within the skin-fold (*carma-puṭa*). *Nakulākṣaḥ* refers to one whose eyes are like those of a mongoose (*nakula*).

Ulūkākṣa (owl-eyed) means having eyes like those of an owl; [it may also mean] kapilākṣa (tawny-eyed) because of the tawny color of the eyes, or rakṣākṣa (protector-eyed), or one with symmetrical eyes.
That part of the eye which is situated near the outer corner (apāṅga) is, for him, situated near the nose;
and that [part] meets the apāṅga situated near it.
He whose eyes are turned away from each other is one with inverted eyes;
he whose eyes are joined together at the bridge of the nose is one with closed eyes.
*Śikyākṣa*: one whose eyes are extremely long, like a hanging loop (*śikya*).
*Kaśmīlitākṣa*: one whose eyelids are closed because the eyelashes have fallen out, so that blood flows from the corners of the eyes like wine.
*Akṣākṣa*: one who has eyes within his eyes; that is, one who has eyes upon his two [existing] eyes.
In the compound *akṣiśāla-śantra-dardru-vicarcikā*, the word *akṣi* is applied as a prefix to each member:
*akṣiśālaḥ*, *akṣiśantraḥ*, *akṣidardruḥ*, and *akṣivicarcikā*.
He whose eyes are exceedingly large is Viśālākṣa.
"Pīta-avadāta-rakta-nāḍī-karṇaḥ" is an instance where the word *karṇa* is applied distributively [to each preceding term]: *pītakarṇaḥ*,
*avadātakarṇaḥ*, and *raktakarṇaḥ*.
"Nāḍīkarṇa" means "one whose ear is like a tube."
The word *kacchu* is connected with each of the preceding terms— *kaṇḍu*, *piṇḍa*, and *sthūlaka*— thus forming: *kaṇḍukacchu*,
*piṇḍakacchu*, and *sthūlakacchu*.

Regarding the term *aṇḍalāṅgulapraticchanna*: it means that his tail (*lāṅgūla*) is covered by the two testicles (*aṇḍābhyām*); thus, because his tail is covered by the two testicles, he is called *aṇḍalāṅgūlapraticchanna*.
Alternatively, because his tail is covered by the two testicles, he is *aṇḍalāṅgūlapraticchanna*.
Regarding the phrase "dull-witted, tongueless, with one hand and one foot":
by the term "dull-witted," the fact that he does not know [the requirements for] full ordination is included.
"Without a tongue" refers to one who is deprived of a tongue.
"Dumb and deaf": by the mention of "dumb," one who is unable to speak despite possessing a tongue is meant;
otherwise, such a person would have been called "without a tongue," as has already been stated for another case.
In the expression "one hand and one foot" (*ekahastapādaḥ*), the word "one" (*eka*) is connected to each of the words "hand" and "foot" individually: namely, "one hand" (*ekahastaḥ*),
"one foot" (*ekapādaḥ*),
and "without hands and feet" (*ahastapādaḥ*).
Regarding the term "blue-haired" (*nīlakeśa*): "blue" (*nīla*) refers to that which has not become green (*aharitabhūta*); therefore, by the mention of "green," blue is already included.
In the compound *hasti-aśva-śva-go-meṣa-mṛga-matsya-ahi-dīrgha-bahuśīrṣa*, the word *śīrṣa* (head) is connected with each preceding term: *hastiśīrṣaḥ*, *aśvaśīrṣaḥ*,
*śvaśīrṣaḥ*,
*gośīrṣaḥ*.
Arambha (the Ram-headed),
Mṛgaśīrṣa (the Deer-headed), and Matsyaśīrṣa (the Fish-headed).
Ahiśīrṣa, Dīrghaśīrṣa, and Bahuśīrṣa.
As for that which is also recited— "all blue, all yellow, all red, all white"—
this too is stated to be [described] by means of the four colors of the elements (bhūta).
"Like one whose neck is severed by a bolt, his bodily postures are severed by the pain of the stake."
(636) And [the same applies] when [the theft is committed] by a thief against a bandit.
The term "being projected" (*ākṣiptatva*) is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
Its nature as an evil course of conduct (*pāpavṛtti*) is stated in general terms.
But is it not the case that there is no distinction between this [course of conduct] and that [evil action]?
For even a thief who has not become a plunderer is one who takes from others with compassion; he is,
for the most part, one who does not take anything at all, or one whose intent is directed toward the non-destruction of life.
And a *dasyu* who has not become a thief, such as a pitiless executioner and the like—
therefore, his status is indeed distinct from that [of a regular thief].
(c) Anujñā (637): When there is the intention of the father, the king acts with authorization as if he were the father himself.
The meaning is that one who has been permitted by the king because he intends to become a father should be regarded as having already been permitted by both parents;
thus, there is no fault when one has gone forth with the king's permission.
(638) In the cases of embracing, permitting, retaining, and announcing [the Dharma], they possess the status of a father.

Even though they lack the status of biological progenitors, the state of being "mother" and "father" applies to those who, having taken them in, maintain them, grant them permission, sustain them for seven days, and announce [the birth] to the Saṃgha;
the meaning is that it does not apply only to those who maintain them by virtue of being biological progenitors. First, regarding the "adopted son" (putrakṛtaka):
Venerable sir,
when they grant full ordination,
from whom should he be dismissed?
"—he to whom [she] has attained the state of being a son; likewise, Dhītikṛtikā has attained the state of being a daughter-in-law to him"—thus ends the passage.
(639) There is no [rebirth] for the two non-human destinies.
The phrase "paternity [is established] in the cases of permission, retention, and delight" is to be supplied [to each].
“Venerable sir, as for one whose mother and father have both passed away...”
"Or if he has entered the animal realm—
is the entire Saṅgha to be consulted for the shaving of his hair?"—
"Certainly not, Upāli," so it is said in that text.
(640) Therefore, there is no arising from immediate succession.
From the two fathers who have gone to the realm of non-humans, there arises an immediate transgression.
(641) This [is] from both parents, even when their sexual characteristics have been transformed.
Even if one is impotent, yet possesses the female nature derived from the mother, there arises the immediate succession [of the offense].
(642) This is the reality regarding those who commit matricide and other such acts.
This constitutes the state of having committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*);
namely, that the ordination of those such as matricides is prohibited—therein, the state of being an ānantarya-perpetrator must be understood.
Thus, it is further stated: "One who has committed an immediate transgression is not to be ordained."
It is not the case that everyone who kills his mother is ineligible for ordination;
thus, the ordination of one who has killed a mother belonging to the animal realm is not prohibited.
(d) Confusion:
In what case does the status of being a defiler of a nun arise for a monk, and the status of being a defiler of a monk also arise for a nun?
In what sense are these two so? He says:
(643) The state of being a corrupter belongs to those who relish unchastity while remaining unconquered.
“By how much, venerable sir,
is one to be called a defiler of a bhikṣuṇī?—
by that which is unchaste conduct.”
"Upāli, a bhikṣuṇī is defiled"—this is the textual passage.
What is it that constitutes the arising of these two mental states? He says: [it is the emission of semen].

The dual number is used here for the purpose of demonstrating that the status of being a "corrupter" (dūṣakatva) arises not only in the two who enjoy [the act], but also in the one who is approached (gamya) and in the one who approaches (gantṛ).
However, the emergence of its status as a defeater does not occur through the presence of a counter-example (*pratiyogitva*) when combined [with other factors];
for there is no connection between one thing and another's defect.
Thus, the presence of a counter-example is not an essential factor (*anaṅga*) in this case.
Furthermore, because it would follow that the fault-finder could not even arise when there is no passion or corruption,
the statement "according to one's desire" (chandaśaḥ) is the scriptural authority (āgama) in this matter.
The meaning of "by one's own will" is as follows:

even when one has been defeated (*pārājita*), does the status of being a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) still exist? Furthermore, in that state, does one possess the quality of being an offender (*dūṣaka*) by defiling these two [the Saṅgha]? (VinSū 59)
He said: Regarding the state of being unconquered, the text here says:
"First, O Venerable One, there are eight..."
If individuals defile a bhikṣuṇī by means of individual objects,
should that bhikṣuṇī be declared defiled? Upāli, she should be declared defiled.
Which individuals therein should be called "corrupters of nuns"?
He replied: "None at all.
For whether in the act of causing a fall or in the act of enduring [the act], the nun remains unconquered; thus indeed is there the recognition of her being uncorrupted.
How then?
When she has lain down on her side or is bent over.
If she does not claim ownership, then during the acts of rubbing,
stroking, and entering,
even if he has brought her down, there is no taking possession by her because of that bringing down.
Or when she herself touches the body of a man,
it is an offense against a man.
Arhatship [is lost] upon entering the state of a woman who is inferior [to a man] in regard to the going forth, the full ordination, and the attainment [of the fruit].

Having renounced the training and entered into a low state of life as a woman, when one undergoes a change of sexual characteristics and attains masculinity, one attains Arhatship through both the going-forth and full ordination;
the meaning is that, unlike in the state of femininity, there is no non-Arhatship.
And [the offense] is an exclusive *pārājika* for one who has committed it.
"Arhatship [is attained] upon the going forth and full ordination; [it is attained] by a man who has reached [the state], and by a woman who has fallen [from it]"—this is the connection.
(646) The status of being a constituent factor [of the offense] applies when resident nuns confer full ordination upon women.

Regarding the *Poṣadhavastu*, the text here says: "As it was said by the Blessed One, 'The state of being a nun must be sought by nuns in the presence of monks,' in the presence of which monks? [It is] in the presence of those monks who are residents and permanent inhabitants, Upāli.
Thus, the dwelling of the nuns is dependent upon the community of monks residing in that very place.
Then, because of seeking instruction and admonition from time to time,
and because transgressing one's reliance is not appropriate— this is what constitutes knowledge.
In this context, the status of being a resident is indeed more firmly established.
When it is being differentiated, the state of non-existence does not remain established.
Let there be the destruction of this upon its abandonment.
"Becoming" (*bhavadbhāvya*) means the state of being in the process of arising (*jāyamānatva*).

When a restraint (*saṃvara*) is being grasped, its "becoming"—that is, its state while remaining in that condition—is subject to abandonment through renunciation and so forth; upon such abandonment, its destruction occurs.
This "propulsion" (*āvedha*) of the restraint is precisely its state of being in the process of arising.

Furthermore, no reversal of the restraint (*saṃvara*) is observed in Āneṅgha’s case regarding jumping and so forth. Therefore, for one who might think that there is no reversal of his restraint because it was not produced [in the first place], this sūtra is intended to prevent such a misconception.
In the *Muktaka* [Vinaya] collection, the text here states: "First, he is ordained..."
Upāli, one who claims to have taken the lay vows should be said to be unordained;
how much more so one who is in the process of being ordained?
The section on ordination consists primarily of questions concerning the state of one who has gone forth.
In the Vinaya-vṛtti [by way of its own commentary], the Pravrajyāvastu is completed.
